title: Ultium Cells retrofits Tennessee plant for LMR cell production - electrive.com
content:
Ultium Cells plans to convert its battery cell plant in Spring Hill, Tennessee, USA, to produce prismatic LMR cells. The new cell chemistry is set to be used in future General Motors electric vehicles starting in 2028, offering approximately 33 per cent higher energy density than LFP at similar costs.
Spring Hill to manufacture prismatic LMR cells for GM starting in 2028.
Image: General Motors
The joint venture between General Motors and LG Energy Solution is set to begin retrofitting work later this year, with he conversion expected to be completed by 2028. According to Ultium Cells, Spring Hill could thus become the world’s first plant to mass-produce prismatic LMR cells.
LMR stands for lithium-manganese-rich, a chemistry featuring a high manganese content in the cathode. GM and LG Energy Solution view this as a middle ground between cost-effective LFP cells and energy-dense high-nickel chemistries. Ultium Cells claims around 33 per cent higher energy density compared to LFP at similar costs. However, the company does not provide specific energy density figures.
The new cells are intended for use in future GM electric vehicles. As early as 2025, GM and LG Energy Solution had announced their plan to bring
prismatic LMR cells
to market maturity by 2028. At the time, the primary focus was on their use in electric pickups and large SUVs.
Ultium Cells aligns Spring Hill with new strategy
The retrofitting of Spring Hill aligns with a broader reorganisation of GM’s battery strategy. In June, the company’s battery chief, Kurt Kelty,
that LMR could play a central role in the portfolio in the future, and LFP might no longer have a place in electric vehicles.
The LFP cells produced in Spring Hill since June 2026 are intended for stationary energy storage systems by
LG Energy Solution Vertech
and not for electric vehicles. For vehicles, GM is now focusing more on LMR as well as continuing to use high-nickel cells for particularly long-range models.
However, LMR technology is not yet fully mature. Current challenges include durability, capacity loss, and limited fast-charging capability. GM and LG Energy Solution have been working on manganese-rich cell chemistries for years.
In the future, Spring Hill is set to unite multiple cell chemistries and formats under one roof. In addition to LMR and LFP, Ultium Cells will also produce high-nickel cells there; both pouch and prismatic cell formats are to be manufactured. Investments in the programmes and further site measures are expected to total around one billion US dollars by 2030. The retrofitting is also expected to create 500 new jobs. The site currently employs around 1,200 people.

title: Vianode and FAAM report successful graphite recycling from battery waste - electrive.com
content:
Norwegian battery material specialist Vianode and Italian battery manufacturer FAAM have demonstrated how waste graphite from battery production can be recycled into high-performance anode material. Both parties now aim to scale their approach for industrial use.
Image: Vianode
As part of a joint development programme,
processed graphite concentrate – recovered from anode production waste at
battery manufacturer FAAM
– into new battery material. According to Vianode, subsequent tests have shown that the recycled product “electrochemical performance comparable to virgin graphite materials”.
In the project, Vianode contributed its manufacturing technology for synthetic graphite, while FAAM provided its expertise in battery production. The partners describe their demonstration as another step towards solving one of the battery industry’s biggest circular economy challenges: recovering and reusing graphite while maintaining the performance, purity and consistency required for lithium-ion batteries.
Building on the results now presented, the companies aim to expand their collaboration to scale the recycling process for industrial use and further integrate recycled graphite into battery production. According to an accompanying statement, the goal is to enable a circular solution that improves resource efficiency, reduces waste and strengthens regional battery supply chains.
Background: While recycling infrastructure for battery metals such as nickel, cobalt and copper is advancing, graphite recycling remains a complex challenge. “Due to stringent requirements for material purity and battery performance, large-scale recovery and reuse of battery-grade graphite has remained limited,” states Vianode’s headquarters in Oslo. However, the current collaboration demonstrates a viable path to closing this gap.
“This collaboration demonstrates that graphite recycling can be both high-performing and scalable,” said Stefan Bergold, CCO at Vianode. “By leveraging our proprietary graphite technology, we can return production scrap directly back into the battery value chain without compromising quality. It also demonstrates the importance of European companies joining forces to strengthen regional supply chains and accelerate the transition to a more sustainable battery industry.” The Norwegian battery material specialist
also intends
to work closely with the German battery recycling company Cylib in this context.
Andrea Civitillo, CEO at FAAM, adds: “This achievement confirms that circularity for graphite is no longer a theoretical objective, but a concrete and scalable industrial reality. By combining our manufacturing expertise with Vianode’s advanced materials technology, we are demonstrating that production scrap can be reintegrated into the process without compromising performance.”

title: Gotion targets 400 Wh/kg solid-state batteries - electrive.com
content:
Gotion High-tech has unveiled new targets for its solid-state batteries. The Chinese cell manufacturer, in which Volkswagen has a stake, is aiming for an energy density of 400 Wh/kg for its Jinshi cells and long-term costs of approximately US$150 per kWh.
Gotion plans a 2-GWh production line for its solid-state batteries.
Image: Gotion High-Tech
At the World Manufacturing Convention 2026 in Hefei, battery manufacturer Gotion highlighted further progress in the industrialisation of its all-solid-state batteries – and unveiled its latest target values.
According to
CarNewsChina
, the firm has set an energy density target of 400 Wh/kg for its solid-state batteries. Previously, Gotion specified a target of 350 Wh/kg for its sulfide-based solid-state cells. However, it remains unclear when this new benchmark will be achieved in near-series production cells. Gotion has also set a more concrete cost target: in the long term, its solid-state batteries are to enter the so-called “one-yuan era”, meaning around one yuan per watt-hour or approximately US$150 per kWh. According to media reports, this would still be significantly higher than the current average prices of Chinese LFP cells.
The current state of development builds on several previous steps. As early as 2025, Gotion had commissioned a pilot production line with an annual capacity of 0.2 GWh. The all-solid-state cells produced there had already been integrated into vehicles and tested on the road, according to the company. For that cell generation, Gotion cited an
energy density of 350 Wh/kg.
Gotion moves closer towards production
In 2024, the company announced plans to start small-scale production in 2027 and aim for mass production by 2030. Since then, the timeline has progressed further: in March 2026, Gotion finalised the design for a solid-state battery production line with an annual capacity of 2 GWh, according to CarNewsChina.
In parallel, Gotion is expanding its materials expertise. At the beginning of 2026, the battery manufacturer agreed on a
collaboration with BASF
on high-performance materials for solid-state batteries. Both companies explicitly aim to address technical bottlenecks on the path to commercialisation and jointly explore opportunities for a future market launch.
Gotion also points to further safety tests of its cells. In puncture and high-temperature tests, these cells reportedly produced neither smoke nor flames. The Chinese group is one of the country’s major battery manufacturers and operates 20 production sites worldwide. In August 2026, Gotion reached 4.61 GWh of installed battery capacity, ranking fifth in the Chinese market according to
China EV DataTracker
. Volkswagen is the largest shareholder in Gotion and
plans to strengthen its ties with the Chinese partner in Europe as well
: a mega-deal based on three joint ventures is also envisaged.

title: Battery shortage: Stellantis pauses EV production in France - electrive.com
content:
Automobile
Stellantis is halting production at its French plants in Sochaux, Rennes, and Mulhouse for at least one week. In two cases, this is due to shortages in the supply of EV batteries, as supplier ACC struggles to keep up with demand for its nickel-based long-range batteries.
Image: ACC
According to
, the plants in Sochaux and Rennes are temporarily halting production due to a shortage of ACC batteries. The news agency cites an official company statement. However, the pause is only indirectly related to the lack of large batteries. Stellantis primarily wants to avoid producing too many other vehicles to “avoid ​building up vehicle inventory that does not match customer demand,” as the company explains. After all, demand is particularly high for long-range electric models, which customers currently face very long wait times for.
The Sochaux plant in eastern France, which produces models such as the Peugeot 3008 and Peugeot 5008, is set to pause operations specifically from 23 to 30 October. The Rennes factory, meanwhile, will close from 22 to 30 October. This is where the Citroën C5 Aircross is manufactured, among others. The previously announced production halt in Mulhouse from 15 to 30 October is said to have other reasons unrelated to the battery shortage.
What is clear, however, is that supplies from
remain a significant bottleneck for Stellantis production. ACC is a joint venture between Stellantis, Mercedes, and TotalEnergies, which originally planned to build three plants in France, Germany, and Italy but is now focusing on the ramp-up phase at its only cell factory in Douvrin, France. The other two major projects
have been scrapped
Bloomberg
reported in February, citing internal sources, operations in Douvrin have also not been smooth. At the beginning of the year, ACC was reportedly only able to equip around 1,000 cars per month with long-range batteries, far below the original target. The joint venture is said to have subsequently brought in a team of experts from China to boost production and reduce high defect rates. Stellantis, as ACC’s anchor customer, is the main party affected by the slow scaling.
In February, ACC also acknowledged fundamental issues: “The ramp-up is proving difficult, but we are learning every day and doing our utmost to serve our customers as best as possible,” ACC Secretary-General Matthieu Hubert told
Bloomberg
at the time.
Stellantis uses the battery cells from the ACC factory in Douvrin, among other models, in electric vehicles based on the STLA Medium platform, including the Peugeot
E-3008 and E-5008
, as well as the Opel Grandland Electric and DS N°8. For these vehicles equipped with ACC cells, Bloomberg already reported delivery delays of up to eight months in February.
In April, a report by
Automobilwoche
then revealed that
private customers in particular are facing very long waits for their long-range models
. The article specifically focused on the corresponding variants of the Opel Grandland, Peugeot e-3008, and e-5008. “Our deliveries have been pushed back to the first or second quarter of 2027,” a Stellantis dealer told the trade journal at the time. Other dealers reportedly no longer received any binding delivery dates.
The situation is particularly awkward for Stellantis brands: after all, it only affects customers who are willing to pay nearly €5,000 more for a larger battery with 97 kWh instead of 73 kWh capacity and the corresponding increase in range, compared to the same model with a smaller battery.
In the meantime, ACC is said to have reduced defect rates and further stabilised production. However, “Unfortunately we are not yet receiving enough of the batteries, despite big progress in ACC’s production,” a Stellantis spokesperson told Reuters in the context of the announced plant pauses. Demand for long-range models, particularly among fleet customers, remains high and continues to exceed current supply.

title: Leclanché files for insolvency for two German subsidiaries – Batteries International
content: Swiss energy storage group Leclanché has filed a “precautionary” insolvency application for its two German subsidiaries, Leclanché GmbH and Leclanché Services GmbH, saying both units faced a cash shortfall. The move, announced on September 23, follows months of financial uncertainty across the group — which has already been told by regulators to publish its long-delayed annual report for 2025 by September 30 (today) at the latest. Leclanché said the insolvency application, made under the German Insolvency Code, was in response to the “illiquidity situations” of both subsidiaries. “The insolvency petition was filed purely as a precautionary measure, as it has not yet been possible to secure further funding for the companies in good time. “Should funding be obtained at short notice and the grounds for insolvency be resolved as a result, it may be possible to withdraw the insolvency application. This would allow the company to continue its operations without the constraints of formal insolvency proceedings.” Leclanché said it continues to have discussions with customers that have indicated a willingness to provide further support, as well as with strategic partners and potential investors. The group said its customer order book remains strong and has grown in recent months. However, Leclanché said it continues to face significant short-term financing, cash and production-capacity constraints. Trading in the group’s shares remains suspended following a September 10 decision by SIX Exchange Regulation, which regulates and monitors exchange participants and issuers on the Swiss Stock Exchange. Leclanché told SIX previously it needed more time to demonstrate it was a going concern, at least until June 2027. Vianode and FAAM advance industrial-scale closed-loop recycling of battery-grade graphite
Oslo, Norway, September 29, 2026 — Vianode, an advanced battery materials company, and leading European energy solutions provider FAAM have successfully demonstrated the recycling of graphite from battery production scrap into high-performance anode material, marking an important step toward establishing a circular value chain for battery-grade graphite.
The collaboration combines Vianode’s proprietary synthetic graphite technology with FAAM’s battery manufacturing expertise to address one of the battery industry’s most significant circularity challenges: recovering and reusing graphite while maintaining the performance, purity, and consistency required for lithium-ion batteries.
As part of a successful development and qualification program, Vianode processed graphite concentrate recovered from FAAM’s anode production scrap and converted it into recycled anode-grade graphite. Testing demonstrated electrochemical performance comparable to virgin graphite materials, confirming the potential for high-value recovery and reuse of graphite within battery manufacturing.
Building on these results, the companies are expanding their collaboration to scale the recycling process toward industrial deployment and further integrate recycled graphite into battery production operations. The objective is to enable a closed-loop solution that improves resource efficiency, reduces waste, and strengthens regional battery supply chains.
While recycling infrastructure for battery metals such as nickel, cobalt, and copper continues to advance, graphite recycling remains one of the industry’s most complex challenges. Due to stringent requirements for material purity and battery performance, large-scale recovery and reuse of battery-grade graphite has remained limited. The Vianode-FAAM collaboration demonstrates a viable pathway to closing this gap.
Stefan Bergold,
CCO at Vianode, said:
This collaboration demonstrates that graphite recycling can be both high-performing and scalable,
“By leveraging our proprietary graphite technology, we can return production scrap directly back into the battery value chain without compromising quality. It also demonstrates the importance of European companies joining forces to strengthen regional supply chains and accelerate the transition to a more sustainable battery industry.”

CEO at FAAM, said:
This achievement confirms that circularity for graphite is no longer a theoretical objective, but a concrete and scalable industrial reality
“By combining our manufacturing expertise with Vianode’s advanced materials technology, we are demonstrating that production scrap can be reintegrated into the process without compromising performance. The companies will continue working together to scale the technology and explore additional opportunities to increase circularity and resource efficiency in battery manufacturing.

title: Europe’s battery capacity won’t meet IAA localisation demand, new study shows - ACEA - Batteries News
content:
Europe’s battery capacity won’t meet IAA localisation demand, new study shows – ACEA
A new study by Mobility Global, commissioned by ACEA, assesses the preparedness of Europe’s battery supply chain to meet the localisation requirements envisaged under the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA).
Under the proposed IAA, battery localisation requirements would be introduced in two phases: six months after entry into force of the text (around 2027-2028), batteries would need to contain three EU-origin components, including battery cells. Three years after adoption (around 2030-2031), this would increase to five EU-origin components, including battery cells, the battery management system (BMS) and cathode active materials (CAM).
The analysis examines how these requirements could shape demand, and the scale of local production required over the coming decade. Three scenarios are considered, each involving a different level of demand for European-made batteries:
Full market (high demand scenario): covering the electric light-vehicle market, including private buyers benefiting from purchase incentives.
Public led (moderate demand scenario): covering the electric light-vehicle, except private buyers, meaning corporate cars, rentals, fleets, dealers, and public procurement.
Public core (low demand scenario): focused on corporate cars and public procurement only.
In all scenarios, supply is not expected to catch up with demand despite European battery cell production’s expected growth to 306 GWh by 2032.
Limited supply will remain the key constraint to expanding the number of cars that would be eligible for “made in the EU” incentives. For example, around 3 million cars may be unable to qualify for the associated incentives because of the lack of supply if the IAA enters into force in 2028.
For medium- and heavy-duty commercial vehicles, the challenge is even more pronounced. The supply-demand gap continues to widen through 2032, reaching 23 GWh, with demand around four times available European supply.
Challenges extend beyond capacity
The findings also highlight deeper structural obstacles to battery localisation:
Most planned European gigafactories are geared towards NMC battery chemistry, while demand is increasingly shifting towards lower-cost LFP batteries, a chemistry-mix dominated by China.
European-made cells remain significantly more expensive than those imported.
Announced production capacity continues to face financing, permitting and implementation risks. Announced capacity should not be considered equal to operational capacity.
Further upstream, Europe faces persistent shortages of cathode and anode active materials (CAM/AAM), with the analysis suggesting that this deficit may not close until 2038-2040, even under a lower-demand scenario.
The findings underline the need for a realistic and economically viable approach to localisation. The effectiveness of the IAA will ultimately depend not only on the ambition of its localisation requirements, but also on whether Europe can build the upstream capacity, competitive operating conditions and investment framework needed to deliver them in practice.

title: China unveils 5-year battery plan targeting large-scale all-solid-state use by 2030 - Batteries News
content:
China unveils 5-year battery plan targeting large-scale all-solid-state use by 2030
China has prioritized breakthroughs in all-solid-state technologies to accelerate the roll-out of next-generation batteries.
The plan also calls for improving sodium battery performance and supporting corporate mergers and restructuring.
China aims to achieve initial large-scale use of all-solid-state batteries by 2030, accelerating the transition of next-generation battery technology from research to commercialization.
The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) on Monday released its new battery industry development plan for the fifteenth five-year period, setting a roadmap for 2026 through 2030.
The document, dated September 14, was jointly issued by 7 government agencies, including MIIT, the National Development and Reform Commission and the Ministry of Transport.
The plan calls for steady growth in China’s new battery industry through 2030, alongside breakthroughs in advanced electrode materials, new electrolytes and high-end auxiliary materials.
Beyond the all-solid-state battery deployment target, it sets goals for long-life lithium batteries to reach 15,000 charge-discharge cycles and for leading manufacturers to achieve product defect rates at the parts-per-billion (PPB) level.
All-solid-state batteries are a key technological priority. The document calls for faster breakthroughs in commercialization technologies, focusing on improving ionic conductivity and cycling stability while optimizing costs.
Specific measures include improving interfacial contact, extending cycle life, advancing pressure-system engineering and scaling up production of high-performance solid electrolytes.
The plan also calls for combining high-voltage, high-capacity cathode materials with new lithium-metal-based anodes and anode-free designs, while developing manufacturing equipment such as isostatic presses for solid-state batteries.
China plans to build a supply system centered on lithium batteries, complemented by sodium and flow batteries, while strengthening its ability to commercialize all-solid-state and ultrafast-charging batteries.
For sodium batteries, the document emphasizes cost, safety and resource availability advantages, calling for the development of cold-resistant, high-energy-density power batteries and energy storage batteries with long cycle lives.
Industry consolidation and supply chain security are another focus. The document supports corporate mergers and restructuring and calls for faster exploration and development of domestic lithium, cobalt and other mineral resources.
On recycling, the plan requires companies to establish used-battery collection systems aligned with their sales volumes. It also encourages them to build recycling capacity in major export markets where conditions permit.
The document proposes a digital identity management system for products including new energy vehicle (NEV) power batteries, exploring internationally accepted battery passport arrangements and promoting mutual recognition of carbon footprint data.
The battery plan follows China’s September 11 release of its fifteenth five-year development plan for the intelligent connected NEV industry, which targets a 70% share for NEVs in domestic new passenger vehicle sales by 2030.
The earlier automotive plan also called for tighter management of power battery production capacity. The latest battery plan further defines priorities for technology development, manufacturing upgrades and broader applications.

title: Dukosi DK-NFLNK™ Brings Safety, Reliability and Scalability to Traditional Modular Battery Architectures - Batteries News
content:
Dukosi DK-NFLNK™ Brings Safety, Reliability and Scalability to Traditional Modular Battery Architectures
DK-NFLNK™ Contactless Communication Solution is Available for Customer Sampling and Battery Development
EDINBURGH, Scotland, Sept. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Dukosi Ltd, the technology company revolutionizing the performance, safety and sustainability of high-power battery systems, announces the availability of DK-NFLNK™ contactless communication solution for development of safer, more reliable batteries based on traditional multi-channel analog front end (AFE) designs. DK-NFLNK™ is AFE agnostic and provides a simple upgrade path from traditional wired or far field wireless BMS architectures to a highly scalable and robust battery communication solution with no change required to the battery architecture. DK-NFLNK eliminates traditional wiring and fault prone connectors with a single bus antenna and offers synchronous, module-level measurements from the AFEs to the BMS host using Dukosi’s proprietary contactless communication protocol based on C-SynQ
. Dukosi’s novel and highly flexible contactless solution is available for customer sampling and development of battery systems for electric vehicles (xEV), industrial and marine applications, robotics and battery energy storage systems for utility and grid-scale projects, telecom infrastructure and AI data centers
Joseph Notaro,
President at Dukosi, stated:
Dukosi’s unique smart cell monitoring solutions and proprietary C-SynQ communication protocol has gained significant market adoption, and we continue to find new problems that our technology can solve for our customers.
”DK-NFLNK and the Dukosi Cell Monitoring System (DKCMS
) share a common communication foundation, C-SynQ, giving battery designers an easy migration path to full DKCMS-enabled Smart Cell battery designs. As such, we have been able to effectively move DK-NFLNK from the proof-of-concept debuted at embedded world in March towards product availability, with samples for key customers and new DK-NFLNK Evaluation Kits (EVKs) available now. We’re providing customers a cost-efficient upgrade path for modular designs to full DKCMS-enabled Smart Cell batteries in future.”
Dukosi’s DK-NFLNK is an intra-battery communication solution that consists of the DK8503 Node chip, DK8203 System Hub chip, the Dukosi API, and Dukosi’s proprietary contactless communication protocol based on C-SynQ
. DK-NFLNK creates a contactless communication channel between the Battery Management System (BMS) Host processor and a traditional multi-channel Analog Front End (AFE). The DK8503 Node interfaces directly with the AFE via a standard SPI connection and is AFE agnostic. DK-NFLNK transfers data to and from each AFE and the BMS Host processor via the Dukosi DK8203 System Hub through a single bus antenna. The near field communication implementation minimizes RF power levels, simplifying mechanical integration considerations. With inherent electrical isolation through the contactless network, DK-NFLNK delivers wired-like performance in a reliable star-network. The same BMS host processor and DK8203 System Hub can be reused across multiple battery pack designs. A common DK-NFLNK library and API support all configurations minimizing software development and maintenance across the business, while maintaining consistent RF performance. DK8503 and DK8203 are AEC-Q100 certified and designed to be ASIL C compliant.
The Dukosi DK-NFLNK™ Evaluation Kit (EVK) and Graphical User Interface (GUI) is designed to enable battery pack developers and BMS designers to evaluate the advantages of Dukosi technology and discover its ease of integration into existing and future battery pack designs. It supports technology evaluation and initial proof-of-concept development across a growing range of BMS host processors and AFE devices.
DK-NFLNK EVK includes:

Dukosi System Hub unit

All cables included: USB, SPI, bus antenna, and coaxial cable
Powerful, yet easy-to-use Microsoft

title: Nuvoton Introduces KA85010UA, Gen 6 26-Cell EIS-enabled Battery Monitoring IC - Batteries News
content:
Nuvoton Introduces KA85010UA, Gen 6 26-Cell EIS-enabled Battery Monitoring IC
KYOTO, Japan, Sept. 29, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Nuvoton Technology Corporation Japan (hereinafter “NTCJ”) announced on September 29 that it will begin providing samples of the KA85010UA, a 26-cell battery monitoring IC equipped with EIS functionality, in January 2027.
The company’s proprietary inductor method reduces the PCB temperature rise during EIS measurements by approximately 93% compared with conventional methods, enabling battery degradation diagnosis, lifetime prediction, and early detection of signs of cell abnormalities. NTCJ also supports integration into applications by providing EIS analysis algorithms.
In addition to battery monitoring functions, this product integrates EIS-based impedance measurement into a single chip. EIS is a technique that superimposes an AC current on a battery and calculates impedance from the resulting voltage and current responses. This makes it possible to perform EIS measurements within the system, without the dedicated measurement equipment previously required, enabling continuous monitoring and diagnosis of internal battery conditions.
This product uses the company’s proprietary inductor method instead of the conventional resistor method, significantly reducing energy loss. Company evaluations confirmed that both power loss and PCB temperature rise could be reduced by approximately 93% compared with the conventional resistor method (Figures 2 and 3).
These low-power and low-heat characteristics facilitate implementation of EIS functionality in automotive batteries and energy storage systems. They also enable stable acquisition of EIS measurement data during operation, charging, and rest, contributing to advanced battery condition monitoring and diagnostics.
Drawing on EIS data-analysis expertise gained through verification with automakers and research institutions, NTCJ provides end-to-end support, from setting up the EIS measurement environment to implementing estimation and abnormality-detection functions and integrating them into applications (Figure 4).
This support allows even customers who are just beginning to use EIS functionality to build battery diagnostic systems more easily and shorten development cycles.

title: Rincell Debuts New Drone Battery Cell at DroneX - Batteries News
content:
Rincell Debuts New Drone Battery Cell at DroneX
The Fremont cell maker makes its European debut in London with an NDAA-compliant tabless 21700 cell rated for 100A continuous discharge and already shipping to drone manufacturers.
Rincell, a U.S. battery cell manufacturer headquartered in Fremont, California, will unveil the RC50T at DroneX, held September 29-30, 2026 at ExCeL London. The show marks the company’s first public appearance in Europe. The RC50T is a tabless 21700 lithium-ion cell built for drones, and it is NDAA compliant. According to Rincell, production is ramping up and the cell is already shipping to customers.
The company designed the RC50T for the high-load phases of a mission: take-off, climb, payload lift and rapid maneuvering. From a standard 21700 cylindrical format, it delivers 100A continuous and 150A pulse discharge, with energy density above 265 Wh/kg (about 120 Wh/lb). Its tabless construction also cuts internal resistance to 3 to 4 milliohms, so more stored energy reaches the motors as usable power rather than heat. In addition, the cell accepts charge at up to 15A for quick turnaround between flights.
Jignesh Parikh,
co-founder and chief executive of Rincell, said:
In an industry often driven by future promises, we chose to focus on proven results.
”For three years we have kept our heads down, taken our cells from the lab into volume production and shipped them to customers. DroneX is the first time we have told that story. Everything visitors will see on our stand is a product they can order and fly today. That includes the RC50T, our highest power 21700 cell, and it is already in the air,”
Shashank Sripad
, co-founder and chief technology officer of PROPEL AERO, said:
The RC50T gives us power headroom, without any loss in energy, that we have not had from a 21700 cell before.
”With internal resistance this low we can build lighter, cooler packs and let the aircraft use more of the energy it is carrying,”
Rincell RC50T and RC50 specifications
The RC50T joins the RC50, a 5Ah 21700 cell already shipping in volume to drone manufacturers across defense, agricultural and surveillance applications. Both cells use silicon-graphite lithium-ion chemistry at a nominal 3.6V, and both operate from -20 to 60 degrees Celsius (-4 to 140 degrees Fahrenheit). By comparison, the RC50 offers roughly 276 Wh/kg, 5C continuous and 10C pulse discharge and a cycle life above 1,000 cycles. The RC50T trades cycle life for power, with a projected life above 500 cycles and a 5.2Ah nominal capacity.
Pricing between the two is comparable. As a result, the choice comes down to the mission: the RC50 where endurance and cycle life lead, and the RC50T where peak power matters most.
Drone builders in the UK and Europe are looking for cells that combine real performance with a supply chain they can trust, and they want them now rather than at some point in the future.
”We are bringing both to London. Our approach is simple: we do not show anything that is not in production, so when we say a cell is available, it is,”
Manufacturing footprint and supply chain
Parikh and Dr. Jagjit Nanda, director of the SLAC-Stanford Battery Center, founded Rincell in January 2023. The company handles research and development in the United States, where it runs a 6,500-square-foot (604-square-meter) pilot line in Fremont. Volume production takes place primarily in India, while a U.S. production facility is scheduled to come online in late 2027. That timeline comes as drone builders face growing pressure on battery supply chains. Rincell is venture-backed and has support from In-Q-Tel, the U.S. Department of War and the California Energy Commission.
Rincell will exhibit on stand U534, showing the RC50T and RC50 alongside sample pack designs.

title: Amprius Secures $75 Million Grant for American High-Energy Density Battery Production - Batteries News
content:
Amprius Secures $75 Million Grant for American High-Energy Density Battery Production
Funds will enable the conversion of an EV battery line operated by a major South Korean battery partner
FREMONT, Calif.–(BUSINESS WIRE)–
Amprius Technologies
(“Amprius” or the “Company”) (NYSE: AMPX),
a leader in high-performance batteries, has been awarded a grant of up to $75 million from the U.S. Department of War (“DoW”) to retrofit an existing domestic production line from EV batteries to high-energy density cells for unmanned aerial systems.
The grant was awarded through the DoW’s Industrial Base Analysis and Sustainment (“IBAS”) program, which funds domestic manufacturing capabilities critical to national defense. The primary objective of this award is to establish high-volume, commercially viable U.S. manufacturing for advanced battery systems that power unmanned aerial systems – Group 1, 2, and 3 drones.
Amprius plans to use the funds to reconfigure an existing U.S.-based electric vehicle battery production line operated by a major South Korean manufacturer. At completion, planned for early 2028, the line is expected to have the capacity to produce 12 million Amprius cells annually. These cells are intended to meet the domestic sourcing requirements of the National Defense Authorization Act (“NDAA”). The conversion project is expected to cost approximately $100 million, including in-kind investments from Amprius and its South Korean partner.
The modified line expands Amprius’ existing contract manufacturing relationships and significantly increases the ability of the Company to provide NDAA-compliant pouch cells for key customers at scale. This project adds to the Company’s global manufacturing network in China, South Korea, and the United States.
Amprius CEO
Tom Stepien
This DoW grant is intended to establish a primary source of domestic, NDAA-compliant battery production,
“Our technology, combined with the U.S. manufacturing prowess of our South Korean manufacturing partner, positions us to accelerate adoption of standardized, high-performance pouch cells in a fast-growing market.”

title: Xnovo Technology Deploys AI-Powered 3D-CT Inspection Solution at the BMW Group’s Cell Manufacturing Competence Centre - Batteries News
content:
Xnovo Technology Deploys AI-Powered 3D-CT Inspection Solution at the BMW Group’s Cell Manufacturing Competence Centre
Automated quality assurance system combines deep learning, analytical image processing, and high-throughput cluster computing to enable production-scale 3D-CT inspection of battery
Press Release
Copenhagen, Denmark
. Xnovo Technology ApS, a pioneer in advanced X-ray imaging and AI-based inspection solutions, announces the successful deployment of its automated inspection tool for 3D Computed Tomography (3D-CT) data at the BMW Group’s Cell Manufacturing Competence Centre (CMCC) in Parsdorf, Germany. The solution enables reliable, high-throughput quality assurance of battery cells directly on the production floor.
3D-CT has long been a leading method for non-destructive inspection, providing detailed access into the internal structure of components. Bringing 3D-CT into a 24/7 industrial production environment is much more demanding: laboratory scans can take hours, while production scans must be completed within seconds. Faster scans lead to more noise, CT artifacts, and lower contrast, which makes conventional inspection workflows less reliable.
A Tailored Solution for the BMW Group
The solution deployed at the BMW Group’s CMCC was developed by Xnovo Technology in close alignment with the engineering teams. Furthermore, the BMW Group’s own analysis methods have been integrated directly into the inspection pipeline. This ensures that the solution is aligned with the BMW Group’s internal quality standards and production workflows.
The solution covers the full inspection workflow. It starts with automated image pre-processing, including beam-hardening correction, volume alignment, and battery component segmentation. It then performs deep learning-based analysis using Xnovo’s proprietary anomaly detection, generates automated reports, and connects with factory data systems through OPC UA and Q-DAS interfaces. Operators get real-time visibility into production quality, while the distributed architecture allows the system to scale with production throughput.
Dr. Stefan Kerscher
, Head of Battery Cell Technology Development, said:
We are delighted with the outcome of this joint project and would like to thank Xnovo Technology for the close and constructive collaboration throughout its development.
”By combining the BMW Group’s expertise in battery production and quality assurance with Xnovo’s strengths in advanced image processing and AI, we have realized a solution that brings automated 3D-CT inspection to production scale. We believe this achievement represents a significant step forward for the industry and establishes a new benchmark for battery inspection software.”
Dr. Sven Gondrom-Linke
, Senior Product Manager at Xnovo Technology, said:
Deploying 3D-CT at production speed is one of the hardest problems in industrial quality assurance.
”The combination of fast scanning, AI-based analysis, and direct integration with the BMW Group’s own processes represents a genuine step forward for the industry,”
Dr. Christian Holzner
, Managing Director at Xnovo Technology, said:
We are proud of the battery inspection solution we have developed and deployed, and of the partnership with the BMW Group that shaped it around production requirements.
”This demonstrates that automated, AI-powered 3D-CT inspection is no longer a laboratory concept, but a production reality.”
Presented at ECNDT 2026, Verona
The technology was presented in a joint talk by Dr.-Ing. Simon Schmid from the BMW Group CMCC and Sven Gondrom-Linke from Xnovo Technology at the European Conference on Non-Destructive Testing (ECNDT 2026) in Verona, Italy. ECNDT is one of the world’s leading forums for advances in non-destructive testing and evaluation.

OCSiAl Technology at the Core of Commercial Electric Flights
OCSiAl’s single wall carbon nanotubes enable battery technologies expected to power the next generation of electric regional aircraft.
The technology supports silicon-rich anodes and dry-coated cathodes, targeting aviation-grade battery cells exceeding 400 Wh/kg.OCSiAl is contributing to the development through a Horizon Europe project bringing together leading battery and aviation innovators
Electric regional aircraft require a new generation of batteries capable of delivering substantially higher energy density without compromising safety. To help make this possible, OCSiAl is contributing its single wall carbon nanotube technology to an ELEVATE project by Horizon Europe.

title: Qnovo Adds Certainty to EV Battery Passports with New Battery Genome Application - Batteries News
content:
Qnovo Adds Certainty to EV Battery Passports with New Battery Genome Application
The application gives OEMs a clearer view of battery health, risk and value than sparse data can provide
MILPITAS, Calif., Sept. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ — Qnovo, a leader in battery intelligence software, today announced it is piloting a new software application built on the Qnovo Battery Genome that gives automakers more certainty about the condition and value of the batteries they put on the road. Used electric vehicles are priced on uncertainty: two batteries of the same age and mileage can age very differently depending on driving profiles, environmental conditions and cell-to-cell variation, and the sparse data available in the aftermarket cannot tell them apart.
That uncertainty is about to have a ripple effect throughout the industry. Beginning February 18, 2027, the EU will require a digital battery passport for every EV battery placed on its market. Battery passports are an important step toward transparency, and for most batteries the basic data they carry will be enough. But a passport built on limited data cannot see a hidden defect or accelerated aging at the cell level. For the automaker certifying that passport, a battery that fails after being declared healthy is a liability, and as more EVs enter service, the number of those outliers grows.
Reducing that uncertainty requires the rich data that exists only inside the vehicle. Together with its automotive OEM partners, Qnovo applies the Battery Genome to the battery’s full electrochemical record, including charging behavior, operating history, environmental exposure and cell-level variation. This software then identifies markers of accelerated aging and hidden defects, projecting how the battery is likely to age. The result is a clearer, risk-adjusted view of what the battery is and what it is not, with residual value as one of its outputs.
Nadim Maluf
, CEO of Qnovo, said:
Battery passports are a welcome step towards transparency, but without a better understanding of the battery, it opens OEMs to liability
“Since the Battery Genome runs in the vehicle where the rich data lives, we know with added certainty what the battery is doing and what it is not doing. That gives the OEM more insight over what is out in the field and more confidence in every assessment.”
As a recognized automotive supplier with software shipping in the auto industry, Qnovo brings the application to OEMs, fleet operators, and insurers as an extension of a stack already deployed, including Adaptive Fast Charging and Health and Safety Diagnostics, and as a natural fit for the software-defined vehicle.

content:
New lithium mine in Cornwall to unlock Britain’s industrial potential and support skilled jobs
Geothermal Engineering Limited will invest around £43 million in a new lithium mine in Cornwall, backed by nearly £10 million through government’s DRIVE35 fund.
New lithium mine in Cornwall will ramp up UK’s industrial resilience, support over 100 jobs and help make Britain better off.
Government is taking action to ensure UK has strong supply of critical mineral to back key supply chains for AI, advanced manufacturing and clean energy sectors.
Investments follows £1bn secured for UK automotive this month alone, supporting hundreds of jobs as part of the Prime Minister’s mission to reindustrialise Britain.
A new mine in Cornwall is set to open as the government ramps up efforts to boost industrial resilience and help secure vital supply chains backing the automotive, clean energy and advanced manufacturing sectors.
Geothermal Engineering Limited (GEL) will invest around £43 million in a new cutting-edge lithium extraction facility in Cornwall. The investment will create nearly 50 direct jobs and support around 80 more across the supply chain, after receiving an Offer in Principle worth nearly £10 million through the Government’s DRIVE35 Automotive Transformation Fund.
The move comes as demand for lithium is expected to increase by 1,100% by 2035 and will support hundreds of jobs and shore up Britain’s supplies of lithium. This critical mineral is essential for powering electric vehicle batteries, which is why the government has now taken action to unlock nearly £230 million of private investment into two lithium projects in Cornwall and Teesside.
With the UK boasting amazing natural resources, and Cornwall at the centre of one of the most important historic mining regions in both the country and Europe – this investment will help unlock the South West’s industrial potential as part of the Prime Minister’s mission to reindustrialise this country.
This builds on Tees Valley Lithium’s £185 million investment to establish one of Europe’s largest lithium refineries in Teesside. This investment will support hundreds of jobs and strengthen the UK’s battery supply chain, following a government Offer in Principle for £18.3 million through DRIVE35.
The investments are made possible by the Government’s Modern Industrial Strategy and represent a major step forward in the UK’s transition to electric vehicles and another strong vote of confidence in Britain’s automotive sector. This is in addition to £1 billion of investment announced already this month from Bentley, McLaren and Nissan.
Business Secretary
Jonathan Reynolds,
Cornwall has a proud mining heritage, and companies like Geothermal Engineering are helping to write its next chapter in unlocking the South West’s industrial potential.
Britain isn’t just a country for innovation and ideas. It’s a country that produces, and we’re building a modern economy rooted in the industries where we’re already strong and that local communities are proud of.
Hot on the heels of over £1 billion of automotive investment secured already this month, this latest win is a big step towards building our industrial resilience.
Dr Ryan Law,
CEO of GEL said:
Lithium is fundamental to the technologies underpinning the automotive sector’s transition to zero-emission vehicles.
At GEL, we are proud to be at the forefront of establishing a new UK lithium industry, demonstrating how Cornwall’s geothermal brine can provide a reliable and sustainable source of this critical mineral.
We believe the UK has an important opportunity to develop the resources, technology and expertise needed to establish a domestic lithium supply, giving the country greater control over an increasingly important raw material and we are proud to be building that capability here in Cornwall, bringing jobs and new investment to the local area.
With commercial production set to begin on GEL’s Cornwall project in 2029, the facility is expected to produce around 1,500 tonnes of technical-grade lithium carbonate from geothermal brine underground each year – enough to power more than 180,000 typical EV car batteries.
The facility has the potential to scale to producing tens of thousands of tonnes in the future, and the lithium produced will give a huge boost to the UK’s EV battery manufacturing, shoring up crucial supply chains and moving Britain forward in the transition towards net zero.
Julian Hetherington,
Automotive Transformation & Engagement Director, APC and Zenzic, said:
The project aligns with the UK’s Critical Minerals Strategy 2035 by expanding domestic production of critical minerals, reducing reliance on imports.
Extracting lithium in the UK is vital for several reasons: it diminishes dependence on supply chains dominated by China and supports the production of electric vehicle batteries, essential for the UK’s transition to renewable energy use in zero emission vehicles.
In addition, the lithium extraction is expected to spark significant economic growth, especially in Cornwall where a vibrant materials cluster is developing at pace, while enhancing resilience by diversifying the supply chain and mitigating risks tied to concentrated global lithium production and processing.
Background
DRIVE35 Offers in Principle to Tees Valley Lithium and Geothermal Engineering remain subject to completion of due diligence and final approvals.
The offers come via the Automotive Transformation Fund, which is part of the UK Government’s DRIVE35 programme, delivered by the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST), in partnership with the Advanced Propulsion Centre UK (APC) and Innovate UK.
The latest investment builds on a wider pipeline of government-backed lithium projects and feasibility studies across the UK.
Recent support through DRIVE35 has included R&D projects led by Cornish Lithium, Watercycle Technologies, Weardale Lithium and Northern Lithium, helping to develop new extraction technologies, scale up domestic production and accelerate commercial deployment.
DRIVE35 is the Government’s flagship automotive programme, providing £4 billion to 2035 in capital and R&D grant funding to unlock transformational private investment and support the sector’s transition to zero-emission vehicles.

title: Redox-Flow Batteries: NMR-EPR for Energy Storage Solutions
content:
Components
Design & Manufacturing
Materials
Testing & Safety
Research
Understand how coupled NMR-EPR spectroscopy advances sustainable energy storage, enabling breakthroughs in AORFBs, CO₂ capture, and environmental remediation.
September 30, 2026
7 Min Read
EPR and NMR are complementary techniques in battery research.
AI illustration generated for Battery Technology.
The growing adoption of renewable energy sources such as wind and solar power has created an urgent demand for large-scale, flexible, and economically viable energy storage technologies, which balance intermittent generation with grid reliability to support net-zero goals.
Redox-flow batteries (RFBs) have emerged as one of the most promising storage technologies: rechargeable batteries that combine chemical tunability with engineering scalability. RFBs store energy in two liquid redox-active electrolytes, one catholyte and one anolyte, housed in external tanks and circulated through an electrochemical cell during operation to convert electrical energy into chemical energy and back. This unique architecture spatially separates energy storage from electrochemical conversion. Consequently, energy and power can be scaled independently, making RFBs particularly attractive for stationary and long-duration energy storage.
In aqueous organic redox-flow batteries (AORFBs), the problematic commonly used vanadium is substituted by an electroactive organic molecule as the energy storage medium. Their cost-effectiveness, flexible design, scalability, and capacity to safely discharge energy for extended periods hold strong potential in developing environmentally sustainable, large-scale electricity grids. However, they can have shorter lifetimes and lower energy density than current commercial vanadium RFBs.
Advancing AORFBs with NMR-EPR to enhance performance and sustainability
Understanding AORFB chemistry holds the key to prolonging lifetime and improving performance. An innovative coupled benchtop nuclear magnetic resonance-electron paramagnetic resonance (NMR-EPR) methodology developed at the Radboud University Nijmegen is being used to investigate the degradation pathways and energy density of advanced electrochemical systems. This article explores how the methodology has broadened understanding of AORFBs, including lifespan and charge/discharge cycles, and has supported the practical deployment of AORFBs in advanced research applications such as carbon capture and per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) remediation.
NMR-EPR benchtop set-up for operando studies of redox-flow batteries. Credit: S. Testa et al., ChemRxi 2025 (CC-BY-4.0 [10.26434/chemrxiv-2025-m5k7k-v2])
Tracking redox processes by coupled operando NMR-EPR
EPR and NMR are complementary techniques in battery research. EPR detects unpaired electrons, whereas NMR investigates the structure, composition, and dynamics of diamagnetic species. The Evan Wenbo Zhao Group at Eindhoven University of Technology/Radboud University focuses on developing operando magnetic resonance methods for studying molecular electrochemistry in renewable energy storage.
Prof. Zhao explains the importance of the coupled NMR-EPR method: “Using EPR, we can look at organic radicals or paramagnetic compounds that are spectroscopically silent to NMR. If there is a diamagnetic species, however, NMR will detect it. Combining the two techniques gives a complete picture of the processes occurring within a sample. This is important in a flow battery system, where the chemistry can evolve from a diamagnetic system to a paramagnetic system and back again. We can detect both.”
There is a body of published work on NMR-EPR combinations, with some researchers using high-field NMR instruments together with a benchtop EPR. However, Prof Zhao believes that the method can have wider application and has pioneered a simpler approach using a benchtop NMR instrument.
He explains that both types of systems are appropriate for research into energy storage materials: “In battery research, low-field benchtop NMR systems are advantageous because they combine flexibility and ease of use with a compact footprint. Positioning the analytical instrument directly alongside the battery system significantly simplifies experimental setup. In contrast, high-field NMR provides excellent sensitivity and spectral resolution and is beneficial when working with low sample concentrations or when overlapping signals need to be separated. However, ferromagnetic materials and samples containing paramagnetic species may be challenging to study at higher fields.”
A flexible tool for RFB research
To make the
operando
experiments more accessible, dedicated control software such as CEEN has been developed to synchronize benchtop NMR, EPR, and electrochemical measurements in a single workflow. This enables time-aligned data acquisition and real-time visualization, helping researchers directly connect spectroscopic changes with electrochemical performance.
Prof. Zhao’s benchtop NMR-EPR technique has been used to monitor the reversible redox reaction of methyl viologen (MV) from the MV²⁺ to the MV⁺• radical in a viologen-based system by linking molecular changes directly to charge and discharge behavior. EPR also revealed radical electronic structure and provided evidence for π-dimer formation, a process relevant to radical stability and battery performance.
The methodology is also being applied to investigate the role of dissolved active species and solid boosters in mediated redox-flow systems.
IMDEA Energy Institute
, in collaboration with the Zhao Group, is studying how solid boosters can increase the energy density of mediated systems by combining the flow architecture of AORFBs with charge storage in solid electroactive materials.
Dr. Marcilla at IMDEA Energy explains: “In a conventional RFB, energy density is limited by the concentration of the active species dissolved in the electrolyte. In a mediated system, dissolved redox mediators shuttle charge between the reactor and a solid booster in the external tank, which enables additional energy storage. Coupled NMR-EPR allows us to track the mediator chemistry and radical intermediates in real time, revealing how charge is transferred to and from the solid booster.”
Understanding degradation and decomposition pathways
Degradation of the organic redox-active molecules is a limitation for almost all AORFBs. Prof. Zhao continues: “Combined NMR-EPR
operando
monitoring let us visualize what is happening within a battery, in terms of how operating conditions influence its degradation and performance. By manipulating the rate of charging or the flow rate, we can extend the battery’s lifetime.”
For example, research has revealed how the decomposition products from dihydroxyanthraquinone (DHAQ) in membrane RFBs can, under certain electrochemical conditions, be converted back to DHAQ. Operando NMR and EPR can therefore be used to hinder side reactions and to distinguish irreversible degradation from electrochemical regeneration pathways.
Alongside this, coupled NMR-EPR is also supporting the development of membrane-free AORFBs. IMDEA Energy has pioneered membrane-free RFBs based on biphasic systems in which two immiscible electrolyte phases create a natural liquid-liquid interface that separates the anolyte from the catholyte, replacing conventional membranes. Dr. Marcilla explains: “Performance of conventional RFBs strongly depends on expensive membranes able to prevent the cross-contamination of active species while providing effective ion transport. These ion-exchange membranes are usually perfluorinated and can contribute substantially to cost and environmental impact. Separating the catholyte and the analyte by thermodynamic partitioning offers an alternative strategy for controlling crossover without the need for ion-selective membranes.”
Dr. Singh explains the role of NMR-EPR in monitoring the success of the membrane-free approaches: “Organic molecules tend to form radical intermediates that may or may not be stable. Our goal is to find out exactly what happens at atomic level and how these processes ultimately affect capacity retention. This wouldn’t be possible without
NMR-EPR to monitor radical formation, chemical decomposition and crossover of the species through the liquid-liquid interphase during operation in real-time.”
Beyond RFBs: CO₂ and environmental chemistry
Understanding electrochemical processes is key not only for RFB research but also for supporting energy sustainability initiatives, such as CO
capture and conversion and NH
synthesis. CO
conversion into value-added chemicals is hampered by low selectivity and stability. The
Liu Group
at Johns Hopkins University uses
operando
characterization techniques to understand the reactions and degradation mechanisms of redox-active organic molecules under real-time conditions.
Prof. Liu explains: “We use inline coupled benchtop NMR-EPR to study organic molecules that are redox-active, changing their state so they can selectively capture and release CO
, ultimately helping manage greenhouse gas emissions. The intermediate molecular species are radicals, which are EPR responsive, meaning the NMR-EPR method gives us unique insight into their fundamental mechanisms. Similar mechanistic insights are also supporting research into environmental remediation, where understanding transient radical species is equally important.”
The Liu Group is also looking at the degradation of PFAS into benign molecules, using electrochemical reduction to break the strong carbon-fluoride bond. Prof. Liu continues: “One of our projects involves chemical transformation from a radical to an EPR-silent species. The NMR-EPR system helps corroborate our hypothesis, allowing us to track the concentration and the reaction timescale precisely.”
Coupled NMR-EPR – Driving research into a sustainable future
Developing improved electrochemical technologies for the future depends on the research going on today to gain a deeper understanding of how redox-active molecules behave under realistic operating conditions. Coupled NMR-EPR spectroscopy enables researchers to follow both diamagnetic species and radical intermediates in real time, providing valuable insight into degradation, crossover, charge-transfer processes, and molecular stability.
Important software developments, such as CEEN, and the use of benchtop instruments further support this approach, simplifying experiments so that synchronized electrochemical, NMR, and EPR data are easily acquired and visualized in real-time. Taken together, coupled NMR-EPR and integrated control software can provide a practical platform for advancing sustainable energy storage, including flow chemistry, electrocatalysis, CO₂ capture, and environmental remediation.

Professor Evan Wenbo Zhao is a tenured Assistant Professor at the Institute for Molecules and Materials at Radboud University, and soon an Associate Professor at the Department of Chemical Engineering and Chemistry at Eindhoven University of Technology. His group focuses on magnetic resonance for electrochemistry and energy materials. He is a Dutch Vidi Awardee and ECS Toyota Young Investigator Fellow.

title: AI and Battery Technology Take Center Stage at The Battery Show
content:

Design & Manufacturing
This year's Battery Show features expanded programming on artificial intelligence in battery design, manufacturing, and testing.
September 29, 2026
6 Min Read
Several panel sessions and keynotes at The Battery Show will discuss the challenges of battery storage and performance in AI data centers.
The Battery Show
The number of sessions at
The Battery Show
have been increasing the past few years as the role of AI in helping to design and manufacture more robust batteries has come into play. This year, the growth of data centers for AI infrastructure has not surprisingly prompted several sessions dealing with issues such as battery storage and transients.
Check out the all the related panel sessions and talks at this year’s Battery Show, taking place at Huntington Place in Detroit October 12through 15.
All times stated are Eastern.
AI in the Battery Space: Monetizing IP, Accelerating R&D, and Building Safer Batteries
Monday, October 12 | 9:00 AM - 12:00 PM | Room 140AB
https://tbsm26.mapyourshow.com/8_0/sessions/session-details.cfm?scheduleid=254
Across three hours and four panels, practitioners who have actually deployed these tools will show what AI is doing today for battery businesses in terms of raising money, shortening development cycles, catching defects, and protecting intellectual property.
The first panel looks at AI tools that map what you have built to the money that wants it: tools that connect your patent portfolio to government grants and contracts, surface potential licensees, and find funding programs companies did not know they qualified for.
The second panel turns to the engineering bench, where large language models and agent-based tools are collapsing multi-day/week/month analyses into minutes, and where digital-thread platforms are changing how manufacturing data is used.
The third panel examines AI-assisted safety and quality testing — what is genuinely faster, what is marketing, and what it costs to deploy on a real line. The fourth panel, led by intellectual property attorneys, covers patent strategy when AI sits in your workflow, and the disclosure mistakes that quietly void protection.
Attendees leave with named tools, real numbers, and a short list of things to do when they get back to the office.
The Future of Battery Manufacturing: Risks and Opportunities in the Age of AI and Cold War Two
Tuesday, October 13, 11:00 AM - 11:30 AM Grand Ballroom B
https://tbsm26.mapyourshow.com/8_0/sessions/session-details.cfm?scheduleid=260
In this keynote session, top-ranked economist, futurist, and bestselling author Jason Schenker examines how AI, reshoring, geopolitical tensions, critical minerals, tariffs, and supply chain risks are reshaping battery manufacturing and investment. Attendees will leave with practical insights on where the greatest opportunities and risks are likely to emerge over the next decade.
AI in Action: Real-World Impact Across the Battery Value Chain
Tuesday, October 13 | 11:00 AM - 11:30 AM | Grand Ballroom B
https://tbsm26.mapyourshow.com/8_0/sessions/session-details.cfm?scheduleid=119
This panel brings together leaders across the battery lifecycle — materials R&D, product qualification, and high-volume manufacturing — to share how AI is integrating into their existing flows and delivering measurable impacts today. Moderated by Voltaiq CEO and Co-Founder, Tal Sholklapper, this session offers a rare cross-functional view into how AI is reshaping battery development and operations—and what it means for the future of the industry.
Each of the panelists will provide a grounded, real-world perspective on where AI is working—and where it’s not. The discussion will cut through the AI hype to discuss the tangible outcomes they are seeing in their respective domains: faster product development, improved throughput, reduced risk, and more efficient high-volume manufacturing.
AI, Data Centers, and the Next Energy Storage Supercycle
Tuesday, October 13 | 1:30 PM - 2:30 PM | Room 140CD
https://tbsm26.mapyourshow.com/8_0/sessions/session-details.cfm?scheduleid=265
The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence is driving unprecedented growth in data center construction, computing infrastructure, and electricity demand. As hyperscale facilities require increasing amounts of reliable, resilient, and continuous power, energy storage is emerging as a critical technology for supporting grid stability, backup power, renewable integration, and future energy security.
This panel will explore how AI is reshaping global energy demand and creating new opportunities for battery storage, grid modernization, and power infrastructure investment. Industry leaders from the energy, data center, utility, and battery sectors will discuss evolving power requirements, the role of energy storage in supporting AI-driven growth, emerging technologies, and the challenges of scaling energy infrastructure to meet future demand.
Attendees will gain insights into the intersection of AI, energy storage, and grid transformation, and why many industry experts view this convergence as the beginning of the next major growth cycle for the energy storage industry.
Batteries Behind AI: The Safety Challenges of Both Distributed and High-Density Energy Storage in Data Centers and how Large-Scale Fire Testing is Changing BESS Deployment
Wednesday, October 14 | 2:00 PM - 2:45 PM | Battery Tech Theater, Booth 6050
https://tbsm26.mapyourshow.com/8_0/sessions/session-details.cfm?scheduleid=334
Chris Unangst will explore the critical role that battery energy storage systems play in supporting the rapid growth of artificial intelligence and data centers, while addressing the unique fire and life safety challenges these technologies present. The presentation will highlight how large-scale fire testing is transforming the understanding of battery hazards, providing valuable insights into thermal runaway, fire propagation, and emergency response. Attendees will gain a practical perspective on how testing data is shaping codes, standards, and risk informed design strategies, enabling safer and more efficient deployment of battery energy storage systems in data centers and other mission critical facilities.
Designing Battery Systems to Manage AI Data Center Power Transients: Architecture, Control, and Validation
Tuesday, October 13 | 3:30 PM - 3:50 PM | Room 141
https://tbsm26.mapyourshow.com/8_0/sessions/session-details.cfm?scheduleid=61
AI-driven data centers produce some of the most demanding power profiles in modern electrical infrastructure. Training and inference workloads generate rapid, high-amplitude load transients that stress utility grids, trigger costly demand charges, and routinely delay facility interconnection by years. Conventional solutions — oversized grid infrastructure, static power correction, or large-format UPS systems — address the symptom at high capital cost without solving the underlying dynamic.
This presentation describes Beam Global's development of a battery energy storage system specifically architected to manage these transients. Fast-response, coordinated multi-timescale control flattens peak demand toward average load — reducing total power allocation required from the utility, shrinking interconnection requirements, and accelerating deployment timelines. The result is equivalent or superior grid-support performance with significantly reduced battery capacity. Beam's proprietary passive thermal management technology enables the aggressive cycling this application demands without compressing battery lifetime.
This work is being conducted in collaboration with the Intelligent Power Electronics at Grid Edge (IPEG) Laboratory at the University of Illinois Chicago, using real-time simulation and hardware-in-the-loop platforms to emulate realistic AI data-center load profiles. Preliminary findings on transient response, thermal behavior, and battery lifetime under high ramp-rate loading will be shared.
AI Meets Battery Science: Accelerating Materials Discovery with Large Quantitative Models
Thursday, October 15 | 2:30 PM - 3:00 PM | Room 140AB
https://tbsm26.mapyourshow.com/8_0/sessions/session-details.cfm?scheduleid=12
Battery innovation is constrained by the enormous chemical design space and the slow design–make–test cycle used in traditional materials discovery. Artificial intelligence alone often fails to generalize beyond available training data, limiting its ability to predict properties for unexplored chemistries. One way to address this challenge is using Large Quantitative Models (LQMs) - an AI-physics framework that integrates machine learning with first-principles simulations to enable accurate predictions across broader chemical spaces.
LQMs combine large-scale datasets, high-fidelity density functional theory (DFT) calculations, and machine-learning potentials to model atomic interactions with near-quantum accuracy while achieving orders-of-magnitude faster computation. This presentation discusses AQVolt26, a largest dataset for halide solid-state electrolytes built from more than 300,000 r2SCAN calculations. The resulting LQM model achieves near-DFT accuracy while reducing compute cost by over three orders of magnitude and accurately reproducing experimental ionic conductivity trends.
The presentation illustrates how AI-physics platforms can dramatically accelerate battery materials discovery and enable scalable exploration of next-generation energy storage chemistries.
Looking Back, Moving Forward: The Evolution of the Battery Industry
Thursday, October 15 | 10:15 AM - 10:45 AM | Grand Ballroom B
https://tbsm26.mapyourshow.com/8_0/sessions/session-details.cfm?scheduleid=297
Join industry veterans Bob Galyen and John Warner in this keynote presentation for a special closing fireside chat reflecting on the evolution of the battery industry and looking ahead to what comes next. The conversation will explore lessons learned, emerging opportunities, and the future of battery innovation and leadership, while marking a meaningful transition as Galyen passes the role of Advisory Board Chairman to Warner.

title: Battery Company’s Move Is ‘A Wake-Up Call for America’
content:
