Industry Outlook
Design & Manufacturing
EnerVenue’s move to China sparks industry debate over the former Secretary of Energy’s post, highlighting US manufacturing challenges and Battery Belt solutions.
September 29, 2026
6 Min Read
The Battery Belt is still in its infancy compared to the mature industrial clusters found in China.
Don Mason/Tetra images/GettyImages
EnerVenue, an American battery startup, recently announced the opening of its first high-volume manufacturing line in Changzhou, China, rather than in Kentucky, sparking a critical conversation about the state of American manufacturing. This move, which dodged a $264 million factory project in Kentucky that would have created 450 jobs, highlights the challenges and missed opportunities in the US manufacturing landscape. Former United States Secretary of Energy Jennifer Granholm’s LinkedIn post on the matter has ignited a wave of responses, shedding light on the systemic issues and potential solutions for revitalizing American industry.
The industrial cluster advantage
Changzhou, where the factory is located, boasts one of the most complete battery supply chains in the world, with around 160 battery-industry companies operating in the city. This ecosystem includes engineers, suppliers, equipment manufacturers, and specialized talent, all located within a 50- to 100-kilometer radius. Such proximity fosters innovation, reduces costs, and accelerates production timelines.
Related:
AI Continues to Rise in Battery Production, Slashing Test Times & Costs
In contrast, the US has improved its battery manufacturing ecosystem, often referred to as the "
Battery Belt
." This emerging industrial corridor spans states like Michigan, Ohio, Kentucky, Tennessee, and Georgia, where companies have made investments in battery production facilities. Companies such as Ford, General Motors, and LG Energy Solutions have established operations in this region, creating a foundation for a domestic battery supply chain.
Toyota Battery Manufacturing North Carolina. Courtesy of Toyota.
However, the Battery Belt is still in its infancy compared to the mature industrial clusters found in China. While individual factories are being built, the surrounding ecosystem of suppliers, workforce training, research institutions, and capital remains underdeveloped. Granholm’s post emphasizes that the goal should not be to win a single factory but to create an environment where entire industries can thrive.
She stated, “I’ve been obsessed with industrial clusters for years. At UC Berkeley, we launched the American Jobs Project to study how states could create good jobs by building clean-energy clusters — not just attracting a factory, but the suppliers, workforce, research and capital around it.”
EnerVenue’s Changzhou facility
EnerVenue
’s Changzhou facility shows a major step forward in battery production. The plant, which began production in September 2026, is the first in the world to manufacture the Aqueous Metal Cell (AMC) at scale. Phase 1 of the facility is rated at 250 MWh of annual capacity, with plans to expand to 1 GWh by 2027 and multi-gigawatt-hour scale by 2028. At full automation, the line is designed to produce approximately 300 fourth-generation AMC units per day.
Related:
$16 Million Prize to Boost US Critical Minerals Workforce
No other company on the market builds an Aqueous Metal Cell, so EnerVenue had to design and build the equipment specifically for the line. Courtesy of EnerVenue.
Henning Rath, CEO of EnerVenue, emphasized the groundbreaking nature of the facility: “The EnerVenue AMC is now being manufactured at scale, that’s what changes today. This is the only facility in the world making this high-performing water-based nickel-based battery; it’s the first battery of its kind that acts like infrastructure rather than a degrading asset.”
According to the announcement, the AMC is built for 30,000 charge cycles, operates in harsh environments, and carries zero risk of fire from thermal runaway. It uses abundant materials, avoids lithium and rare earths, and can recover and reuse its nickel at the end of its life. These features make the AMC a compelling alternative to lithium-ion batteries.
The role of IRA in building US industrial clusters
The EnerVenue story underscores the importance of industrial clusters in manufacturing success. Granholm connected EnerVenue’s decision to broader policy implications, particularly the dismantling of the
Inflation Reduction Act (IRA)
. However, the rollback of these policies has had severe consequences, with EV sales down 36% year over year. And battery manufacturing investment fell 47% in Q1 2026. Granholm argued that tariffs alone are insufficient to rebuild American manufacturing. Instead, a combination of supply-side and demand-side policies is needed to create industrial clusters that can compete with those in China.
Related:
Tapping Battery Compound Production Potential
Voices from the industry: Agreement and divergence
Granholm’s post sparked a wave of responses from industry experts, offering insights into the challenges and opportunities for American manufacturing. These responses can be classified into two categories: agreement with Granholm’s perspective and diverging views.
Agreement with Granholm’s perspective:
Seahum O., a regenerative AI expert, strongly
with Granholm’s emphasis on industrial clusters. She highlighted the Midwest, particularly Ohio, as a historical example of such clusters, citing First Solar as a success story. However, she lamented how America, despite being a pioneer in solar technology, has fallen behind in scaling and innovating clean energy.
“We invented solar in the 1800s, took it to market, and scaled it globally, only to watch the world take it farther while we stalled.”
Linus Beer, a managing consultant at E3,
supported
Granholm’s perspective, emphasizing the role of state-level initiatives in building industrial clusters. He pointed to the Massachusetts Clean Energy Center as a model, noting its grant programs to expand Climatetech test and demonstration sites in partnership with local businesses and research institutions.
Katie Mehnert, CEO in energy and industrials, and John Mossop, a fractional COO and M&A advisor, both
with Granholm’s focus on proximity and industrial clusters. Mehnert noted untapped potential in regions like Houston and the southern US, while Mossop stressed the need to develop the skills America needs to compete globally.
Diverging views
Antonio Reis, a manufacturing and product development professional,
expressed
skepticism about the IRA’s effectiveness as industrial policy. He argued that permitting delays and regulatory hurdles remain significant barriers to manufacturing at scale in the U.S.
“It still takes about two years, and a stack of agency and political work, to permit a metal-finishing line in the U.S. … If the goal is factories, start with permits that have a clock, rules that last the life of a line, and money next to people who have already shipped product.”
Reis also criticized the IRA for funding companies that announced projects without the capability to deliver, likening it to the “shovel-ready” stimulus programs of the past. He contrasted this with China’s approach, where regulatory processes are faster, and state support often offsets operating costs.
John Wind, an expert in decarbonizing chemical processes, took a more
critical tone
, blaming the Trump administration for sabotaging the clean energy industry in America. He argued that while the IRA was a great start, its impact has been undermined, leaving the future of US manufacturing bleak.
“Manufacturing in the U.S. has a very bleak future, except for coal plants, asbestos, and buggy whips, which will be booming.”
EnerVenue’s move to China highlights the challenges facing American manufacturing but also underscores the opportunities for revitalization. The company positions its AMC as a competitive alternative to technologies like pumped hydro, flow batteries, and compressed air, rather than competing directly with lithium-ion batteries on the price per kilowatt-hour. This strategic focus reflects the growing demand for energy storage solutions that prioritize longevity, safety, and environmental sustainability.
Investments in industrial clusters, such as the Battery Belt, will be critical to creating ecosystems that support advanced manufacturing. Additionally, leveraging public-private partnerships will play a pivotal role in ensuring the US remains a leader in clean energy and high-tech industries. By addressing these systemic challenges, American manufacturing can reclaim its position as a global powerhouse.

, blending her engineering background with a passion for technology journalism. She holds a Bachelor of Science in Electrical Engineering from Universidad Metropolitana in Caracas, Venezuela, and a Master of Science in Electrical Engineering from NYU Tandon School of Engineering.
Guerra's career spans power systems engineering, oil & gas consulting, and technical writing and editing. She worked for several years at Kellogg, Brown & Root Ltd. title: Achilles and Saudi Arabia: Supporting ESG in Manufacturing
content:
Achilles and Saudi Arabia: Supporting ESG in Manufacturing
Prioritise Us
on Google
Saudi Arabia chose Achilles as a provider of independent assurance across its manufacturing industry. Credit: Unsplash
Katie Ferrier, Regional Director UKI & MEA at Achilles, explores how the platform is supporting resilience for manufacturing organisations in Saudi Arabia
Saudi Arabia is undergoing major industrial growth, undertaking a plan to develop a sustainable economy as
part of its Vision 2030
The aim of Vision 2030 is to develop strong social infrastructure, a thriving economy which supports businesses of all sizes and a commitment to accountability and efficiency.
As part of this, it has appointed Achilles as one of the providers of supplier audit services for the nation, helping to advance ESG maturity across manufacturing.
A sustainable partnership
In September 2026, Achilles was appointed as a provider of independent assurance and supplier audit services. In this role, it will be supporting the Saudi Ministry of Industry and Mineral Resources' programme, helping
develop sustainable operations
across the kingdom’s manufacturing practices.
This is part of an ongoing relationship between the nation and the risk intelligence platform, building upon the MoU at ‘Made in Saudi 2025’ – the exhibition where local and international companies could sign agreements and plans with government entities. The event is an opportunity for Saudi products to be showcased and new industrial or commercial partnerships to be formed.
At the event,
Achilles signed an MoU
with the government to help drive compliance across its expanding manufacturing sector. Now, this is going one step further, demonstrating a growing relationship and increasing responsibility across the industrial landscape.
"Across global supply chains, organisations are looking for greater confidence that ESG commitments translate into measurable action,” explains Katie Ferrier, Regional Director UKI & MEA at Achilles.
“Our role is to provide independent assurance, trusted data, and practical insights that help manufacturers strengthen performance and build resilience."
Katie Ferrier, Regional Director UKI & MEA at Achilles
Key facts
Since Vision 2030 was launched, more than 1,000 environmental and regulatory reforms have been implemented
1.7 million SMEs operate across the Kingdom
More than 12,900 industrial establishments support downstream activity across manufacturing and advanced industries
Achilles has more than 35 years of risk experience
More than 330,000 global suppliers are actively monitored by Achilles
Developing credibility
Achilles was selected as one of four delivery partners, recognised for its strength in supply chain assurance, supplier engagement and sustainability improvement. As Saudi grows its manufacturing capabilities, the kingdom is looking to develop credibility across its ESG assurance.
The programme is supporting manufacturers by awarding them with certification. Through this, the manufacturers are increasing their competitiveness and will be one step closer to establishing themselves in global networks.
SIDAM, a Saudi non-governmental organisation, is working with Achillles to help manufacturers establish themselves as meeting local ESG goals and international standards.
“For many manufacturers, the challenge is no longer whether ESG matters. It’s understanding how current performance measures up, where the
biggest gaps exist
, and which improvements will deliver the greatest impact,” explains Katie.
“Independent ESG assurance bridges that gap, providing an objective assessment of performance and a clear foundation for continuous improvement.”
This will help Saudi manufacturers gain greater confidence with international customers,
investors and supply chain partners
For many manufacturers, the challenge is no longer whether ESG matters. It’s understanding how current performance measures up.
Katie Ferrier, Regional Director UKI & MEA at Achilles
Saudi Arabia is partnering with Achilles to increase ESG operations | Saudi Arabia. Credit: Getty Images

Achilles
CEO: Sebastien Roussotte
HQ: Oxfordshire, UK
A global provider of supply chain risk management solutions with over 35 years of experience in supplier assurance. The platform actively monitors more than 330,000 suppliers worldwide, delivering independent ESG assessments, supplier qualification services, and compliance verification across critical industries including manufacturing, energy, infrastructure, and construction sectors globally.
SIDAM (Saudi Industrial Development and Marketing)
A Saudi non-governmental organization dedicated to advancing the Kingdom's manufacturing sector competitiveness. SIDAM works collaboratively with international partners to help local manufacturers meet both domestic ESG requirements and international standards, supporting Vision 2030's commitment to developing sustainable industrial practices and global market access for Saudi products.

The governmental body overseeing Saudi Arabia's Vision 2030 industrial transformation programme. title: Range Rover Sport EV orders open at nearly $150,000 with up to 378 miles of range
content:
Range Rover
Range Rover Electric
Peter Johnson
| Sep 30 2026 - 7:36 am PT
Range Rover Sport EV
is bringing new levels of performance with an all-electric powertrain, but it isn’t cheap.
Range Rover Sport EV prices and Range
After launching the flagship Range Rover Electric earlier this month, the luxury brand opened orders for its second fully electric SUV on Wednesday.
The Range Rover Sport Electric is now on sale in the UK, starting at about £110,000, or roughly $146,000.
Like the flagship model, Range Rover promises the Sport EV will match, if not outperform, the current internal combustion engine (ICE) version.
The electric SUV is “first and foremost a Range Rover Sport,” Martin Limbert, the brand’s managing director, said. By using an all-electric propulsion system, Range Rover was able to “unlock new levels of responsiveness and precision,” Limbert said.
Powered by a dual-motor all-wheel-drive powertrain, the setup delivers up to 542 horsepower (550 PS) and 627 lb-ft (850 Nm) of torque, the most any Range Rover Sport has offered to date.
Range Rover Sport Electric (Source: JLR)
In Dynamic Launch Mode, the Range Rover Sport EV can accelerate from 0 to 60 mph in as little as 4.3 seconds.
The electric SUV features “uncompromised all-terrain capability,” Range Rover said, with the ability to wade through 900 mm (35.4″) of water and climb a 45-degree slope.
It’s equipped with advanced tech, including virtual AWD, adaptive dynamics, twin valve dampers, and an electric active roll cage, making it the most dynamic Range Rover Sport in the lineup.
Range Rover Sport Electric (Source: JLR)
The Range Rover Sport EV gets up to 378 miles of WLTP range and up to 333 miles of real-world range using a 118.5 kWh battery.
Based on an 800V architecture with charging at up to 350 kW, the electric SUV can add up to 136 miles (220 km) of driving range in as little as 22 minutes. Charging from 10% to 80% takes about 22 minutes.
Inside, the interior remains very close to the current model, with a 13.1″ curved glass touchscreen running the latest Pivo Pro infotainment system. There’s also a 13.7″ instrument cluster behind the steering wheel.
Range Rover Sport Electric interior (Source: JLR)
Orders for the Range Rover Sport Electric opened in the UK, starting at about £110,000 ($146,000) for the base Dynamic SE trim.
That’s about £44,000 ($58,000) less than the flagship Range Rover Electric SUV, which starts at £154,070 ($200,000) in the UK. Deliveries are scheduled to begin next year.
The Range Rover Sport EV will launch in the US, but when has yet to be confirmed. It’s expected to go on sale sometime in 2027 as a 2028 model. The
Range Rover Electric
starts at $140,450 in the US, so you can expect it to be slightly less, at around $120,000 to $130,000.

title: Tesla Robotaxi fleets are the new crypto treasury for zombie companies
content:
Tesla Robotaxi
Tesla Cybercab
Fred Lambert
| Sep 30 2026 - 7:02 am PT
A pre-production Tesla Cybercab and the steering column bolted inside it, spotted in Berkeley. Photo: Adam Machacek
A Nasdaq-listed company worth about $2.4 million says it wants to buy 500 Tesla Robotaxis. KIDZ AI, formerly an online coding school for kids, announced today that it sent Tesla a “procurement inquiry” for the vehicles and plans an “Autonomous Fleet Operations Strategy.”
If the name doesn’t ring a bell, the playbook should. Tesla’s Robotaxi is turning into what bitcoin treasuries were for failing micro-caps in 2025: a buzzword you bolt onto a dying business to get the stock moving.
A kids’ coding school that keeps pivoting
KIDZ AI used to be called Classover Holdings. It sold online classes to K-12 students and went public through a SPAC merger in 2025.
The education business isn’t going anywhere good. According to the company’s
Q2 2026 results
, service revenue fell 34% year-over-year to $0.48 million, and it lost $2.5 million in the quarter. That’s more than five dollars lost for every dollar of revenue.
So it started pivoting. A lot.
In June 2025, Classover announced a deal for up to $500 million in convertible notes from Solana Growth Ventures, with up to 80% of the proceeds going to buy SOL tokens. It was a textbook crypto treasury play. Only an initial $11 million was funded.
A year later, in June 2026, the company rebranded as KIDZ AI and said it was dropping Solana for the Hyperliquid ecosystem and “yield-bearing stablecoin strategies.” The same month, it announced a push into GPU cloud and AI data centers. Since then, it has announced a $44.6 million, 60-month GPU compute deal, a stake in a data center in Cambodia, a “KIDZBot” robotics financing, and now, a fleet of Tesla Robotaxis.
That’s four hot sectors in about 15 months. Crypto, AI compute, robots, and self-driving cars.
The stock is down 99.97%
The market isn’t buying any of it, including today’s Robotaxi news. KIDZ jumped about 10% in pre-market trading after the announcement, then fell about 6% once the market opened. So much for the pump.
Zoom out and it’s worse. KIDZ stock is down about 99.97% over the last year, and the company’s market cap sat around $2 million.
To stay listed on Nasdaq, it did a 1-for-10 reverse split in June and then
a 1-for-15 reverse split in August
. That’s a combined 1-for-150 in about two months, and both filings cite Nasdaq’s $1 minimum bid price rule.
Now put the Robotaxi order next to that. Tesla hasn’t published a price for the Cybercab, but even at Elon Musk’s own “under $30,000” target, 500 of them would cost about $15 million. That’s roughly six times the company’s entire market value. KIDZ AI reported $8.88 million in cash and restricted cash at the end of June.
To be fair, the company says as much in its own release. The inquiry “does not constitute a binding order,” the plan is in a “preliminary planning, evaluation, and partner exploration phase,” and KIDZ AI “may determine not to proceed.” In other words, it’s a press release, not a purchase.
We’ve seen where betting on Musk’s Robotaxi ends
Earlier this month,
Tesla started circulating an interest form for Cybercab fleet buyers
at its underwhelming launch event, and anyone can now say they “submitted” something to Tesla.
But companies that bought into Musk’s self-driving pitch don’t have a great track record. MisterGreen, the Dutch Tesla-only leasing company, built a fleet of more than 4,000 Teslas partly on Musk’s claim that they were
“appreciating assets”
that would earn robotaxi money. Instead, Tesla’s price cuts crushed resale values, the robotaxi income never showed up, and
MisterGreen went bankrupt
, wiping out its bondholders.
And Tesla’s own Robotaxi service still barely exists at scale.
Its active fleet in Austin
is still extremely limited, not much bigger than where it was at launch in June 2025, while Waymo runs roughly 4,000 driverless vehicles.
Electrek’s Take
Last year, I wrote about
the “zombie pivot”
: companies with shrinking or broken core businesses announcing bitcoin treasuries to juice their stock. Semler Scientific’s chairman literally said his company was in the “zombie zone.” Metaplanet was a budget hotel chain. Classover/Kidz AI, with its Solana treasury, would have fit right in.
Now the crypto trade has cooled, and the new magic word is Robotaxi.
Musk has spent seven years telling people that Teslas will make money on their own, and he’s now
asking fleet buyers to take on the capital risk of Cybercabs
that Tesla doesn’t want to carry itself. When the buyer lining up first is a $2 million kids’ coding school that was a Solana treasury a year ago, that tells you a lot about who this pitch attracts.
If Tesla’s Robotaxi were truly profitable, Tesla would deploy them itself. It wouldn’t sell them to third-party to take the profits. Only zombie companies like Kidz AI can’t see that or ignore it for a stock pump.

title: China's 2,250kW chargers are already in service, while US thinks about 750kW next year
content:
Just last week, Geely announced it would roll out 2.2 megawatt chargers, able to charge an EV in under 5 minutes. Those chargers are now already in service in 5 cities, with 15,000 charging sites planned by the end of next year.
Meanwhile, the fastest upcoming charger in the US, a respectable 750kW, is coming sometime next year, after being pushed back from 2026.
China’s EV industry has been advancing incredibly rapidly, and its EV charging ecosystem is no exception.
The country already has tens of thousands of megawatt-level chargers which can charge an EV in 5-10 minutes, but China’s EV companies are rolling out even faster charging as they compete over seconds, not minutes of faster charging times.
The latest development is Geely’s 2.2MW charger, announced just last week. The company even says that it uses an advanced thermal-control algorithm that helps increase longevity, which is a consideration when you’re pumping so much power so quickly into a battery.
2.2MW might be a bit of a misnomer here, since it’s shared by two charging heads. The charger runs at 1,500V/1,500A, but no cars exist (yet) that can accept a 1,500V charge, so instead two cars can get over 1MW of power simultaneously.
China’s scale and speed are phenomenal
But the real story is the scale and speed at which these developments happen. Geely released a 1.5MW charger in March of this year. Its 2.2MW charger comes just six months after that last development.
Even more impressively, Geely already has working chargers in the wild, just a week after the announcement. CarNewsChina cites National Business Daily and says that Geely’s chargers have already rolled out in five cities: Hangzhou, Shanghai, Ningbo, Jiaxing, and Xi’an.
The same happened when BYD announced its 1.5MW system in March. In just 5 months, the company installed 10,000 chargers. Geely plans a rollout of a similar scale, installing 15,000 chargers by the end of next year.
Geely also announced a partial purchase of NIO’s battery swapping unit, which is a bit puzzling for a company with leading fast-charge technology, but it doesn’t hurt to hedge your bets (well… until battery swapping fails as a concept and Geely’s $2 billion investment goes down the drain, but we’ll cross that bridge when we get there).
Compare to the US, which is both behind and moving slower
Meanwhile, it’s still rare to find even one or two 350-400kW chargers at a US charging station, let alone anything quicker.
We did get some news this week offering a reprieve: EVgo says it will release 750kW charging in America next year, which is about twice as fast as the current state of the art. Those chargers would take about ten minutes to charge an EV, assuming it can accept enough juice (so far, the upcoming Mercedes AMG GT is the only US EV that can handle numbers like that).
EVgo’s 750kW system will also share power between stalls, so we’re not sure what kind of juice it will deliver to each individual stall, but regardless the peak is still quite a lot lower than China’s.
What’s notable about the EVgo announcement is how long it took. It started with a partnership forged in 2024, which predicted availability in the second half of 2026. We’re now in that second half, and yesterday’s press release delayed availability until sometime in 2027.
So in the same amount of time as that delay – a half year – Geely added another 750kW to its already-mega-fast 1.5MW charging system.
As for other quick chargers in the US, the largest system is Tesla’s Superchargers. In 2022, Tesla announced its V4 Supercharger, with 500kW peak power.
It took about three years for the first of those to show up in the wild – the vast majority of Superchargers in the US are still capped at 350kW or lower (which CEO Elon Musk once referred to as a “children’s toy“).
Tesla also has a “Megacharger” system for its Tesla Semi, but that runs at 1.2MW, which is slower than the light-duty consumer offerings from either BYD or Geely.
The US chose to have worse charging
The US could have had a faster charging rollout, as President Biden’s Inflation Reduction Act and Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act built programs to help accelerate the buildout of these chargers.
But those programs have moved slower than they should, for several reasons both at the state and federal level.
The federal reasons have had to do with intentional roadblocks from the republican party, like illegally trying to pause disbursement of funds, dismantling the government office intended to increase efficiency, and making up rules to make it impossible to install faster chargers.
At the same time, republicans have shipped EV jobs to China by canceling Biden-era programs that had led to a renaissance in US manufacturing.
Top comment by OrangeFan
This is playing out like the phone charging cable fiasco except on a much more expensive grander scale. Cars and Charging stations are not disposable items that you throw away every couple of years. It took a long time to settle on USB C type and even then it took Europe basically forcing Apple to finally switch to USB C.
You can't play the same game with EV chargers, Europe is using CCS, United States is switching to NACS....slowly, China is using another connector all together that actually supports higher voltage. And remember, that unlike Gas Pumps, you NEED TO REPLACE charging cabinet with every change in charging speed. They cost a lot of money and companies that are concerned with return on their investment, are not going to rip out relatively fresh installations just to replace them with the next best thing. Likewise, people are not going to throw away EVs and replace them new faster charging ones, especially since EVs last a very long time.
You can blame one party or the other, but don't ignore the facts.
Then there has been the unfortunately bipartisan effort to put up tariffs against China. We may all finally be starting to realize at this point what a bad idea tariffs are for the whole economy, but tariffs on Chinese autos were also expanded greatly by President Biden, and there is currently an effort to ban any Chinese car from even thinking about crossing the border, even as a private vehicle on vacation from Canada or Mexico.
The intent seems to be to hide how advanced Chinese autos are from American consumers, so we don’t realize how much better automotive technology is in the rest of the world, outside of the city-in-a-hole we’ve created for ourselves.
But you don’t win a technology war, or a trade war, by refusing to participate. China is advancing automotive technology rapidly, and those advancements happen whether we’re covering our eyes and ears or not. The only way to compete is to get better, faster. And we’re already behind, so you better start moving faster than China if you want to catch up.

title: IONNA tops 180 charging sites, with discounts for these EV drivers
content:
Rapidly expanding DC fast charging company IONNA now has more than 180 sites open across the US, and EV drivers of four of its founding automakers’ brands can now get discounts when they plug in.
The automaker-backed network, which uses Alpitronic hardware and in-house-developed software, says it has more than doubled its footprint since the start of 2026 and is now the largest 400 kW charging network in the US.
IONNA’s eight founding automakers are BMW, GM, Honda, Hyundai, Kia, Mercedes-Benz, Stellantis, and Toyota. They’re building a charging network open to all EV drivers with sites it calls “Rechargeries.”
More Circle K charging stops
More than 40 Rechargeries have opened at Circle Ks since IONNA announced its partnership with the convenience store chain in April.
As Electrek previously reported, the company aims to bring IONNA charging to more than 350 Circle K locations. That includes around 85 existing fast-charging sites that IONNA will upgrade and operate. The Circle K rollout features 400 kW chargers with both NACS and CCS connectors.
Discounts, without another charging app
Hyundai and Mercedes-Benz have joined BMW in offering IONNA 10% charging discounts through their automaker apps and Plug & Charge as of October 1. IONNA says its remaining founding automakers will follow.
Plug & Charge lets a compatible EV handle authentication and payment when it’s plugged in, so drivers don’t have to start each session through an app.
Volvo drivers now have Plug & Charge support on IONNA, with Toyota and Lexus support expected in October.
IONNA has also added integrations with Presto, ChargeHub, and EV Connect, bringing its supported partner apps to 19. Rather than asking drivers to download an IONNA app, the network is making its chargers accessible through other platforms.
“The industry has treated charging scale and charging quality as a tradeoff. Our growth and first-place customer satisfaction ranking show that drivers can and should expect both,” said Seth Cutler, CEO of IONNA. (IONNA ranked first for DC fast-charging satisfaction in J.D. Power’s 2026 US Electric Vehicle Experience (EVX) Public Charging Study.)
When I asked Cutler what he felt was the biggest challenge facing the company going forward, he replied that it was ensuring quality remained high amid the company’s rapid growth.
EV drivers get a say
IONNA has established a Driver Advisory Council made up of members of the EV community to provide feedback on network performance, customer priorities, and future products.
The Council’s first assignment is gathering feedback on IONNA’s new Driver’s Dashboard, which lets drivers check real-time details of their charging session by scanning a QR code on the charging screen.
The next step reaches beyond the charging sites. Starting in Q1 of 2027, IONNA plans to send ambassadors to its eight backing automakers’ dealerships to teach staff about EV charging – putting that information where shoppers are deciding whether to buy an EV.
I was delighted to hear this news when Cutler told me yesterday, because, based on my own experience with dealerships, there is a lot of room for growth in EV knowledge, which really impacts buyers’ experiences and decision-making.

I rarely charge away from home but in over four years of ownership, my best DCFC experience was last week at an IONNA. Plug and charge, $0.39 per kWh and, for the first time EVER my Mach-E saw 150kw peak charging. In fact, very briefly, charging reached 155kw.
For people with BEVs that charge on the slow side of today's charging curves, reaching your peak can make a road trip just a little bit nicer.

title: The rationale behind the UK's largest compressed air energy storage plan - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
EnergyPathways CEO Ben Clube tells
pv magazine
that the company’s compressed air energy storage (CAES) project in the Irish Sea will enter the second round of the UK’s long-duration energy storage (LDES) support scheme as a more mature bid.
Brian Publicover
30 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
EnergyPathways, which is listed on London’s AIM market, is developing the Marram Energy Storage Hub (MESH) in salt caverns beneath the East Irish Sea, about 18 km off Lancashire, England, with onshore facilities at the Port of Barrow.
The first phase is a 300 MW/55.2 GWh CAES plant, more than seven days at full power, alongside planned gas and hydrogen storage and hydrogen and graphite production. It is currently the largest CAES project under development in the United Kingdom.
The pre-revenue company, which announced a proposed fundraise on Sept. 28, is targeting a final investment decision in 2028 and operations by the end of 2031, subject to consents and Ofgem cap-and-floor support. It did not apply to the scheme’s first window, in which Ofgem provisionally selected 16 projects totaling 7.6 GW and 136.9 GWh in June.
pv magazine
asked CEO Ben Clube why the company sat out the first round and what MESH needs from UK policy.
ESS News: MESH isn’t among the projects in the first round of Ofgem’s cap-and-floor scheme. What happened, and what are you hearing about round two?
Ben Clube:
We didn’t apply for the first round. We were invited to, but we chose not to, so it wasn’t a matter of being picked or not. We’ve already been invited by Ofgem and Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) to participate in the second round of the cap and floor. We’re just awaiting the official launch, but the guidance from government is that the process will launch toward the end of this year.
If the second round slips beyond that, what does it mean for the project?
The cap-and-floor second round has already been pushed back by about six months from the government’s original plans, because of delays in closing the shortlisting for the first round. But it hasn’t stopped the MESH LDES project from proceeding. The project we submit will be much more mature, and we expect to put forward a very mature proposal with the issues and criteria well addressed. The cap-and-floor process is evolutionary: projects mature over the one-year evaluation period. In effect, we’re getting everything done before the process starts.
If cap-and-floor and gas storage support don’t come through in time, is there a version of MESH that still gets built? Which parts would survive: the storage, the hydrogen, the graphite?
MESH has already been recognized as a project of national significance. We’re in regular communication with the government about the project, and the support to see it proceed is very strong. So we don’t see it as a matter of if, but when the government is able to launch the second round.
The first-round cap-and-floor projects barely scratch the surface of the challenge ahead. The first round is about 130 GWh of storage capacity with an average duration of about 18 hours. Compare that to the scale of the challenge, where surpluses each year could be as much as 70 TWh, adding system costs in the multibillions. And because the system is wind-dominated, surplus events are typically well in excess of 12 hours, and often days. The first round isn’t delivering the amount of storage, or the right type of storage, that the UK desperately needs to bring down electricity bills.
What makes the salt formation suitable for caverns?
The salt is a very thick sequence, 500 to 600 meters of vertical relief, and it’s virtually pure halite. That combination of purity, thickness and depth makes it ideal for constructing salt caverns for compressed air storage.
What drives the low-cost proposition of MESH is the large scale of the caverns we can construct. Each cavern will be 700,000 cubic meters, the equivalent of four St. Paul’s cathedrals. There are limited places where this potential exists. The first MESH project requires four of these caverns, but we think the entire license area has potential for up to 60. So the scalability of MESH is immense, and it represents a significant strategic storage asset that can harness a considerable amount of the surplus wind the UK will generate in future.
Is MESH purely a compressed air project, or is there a hydrogen storage element as well?
It’s an integrated storage system. The compressed air captures surplus wind generation, but we combine that with gas and hydrogen storage to provide a strategic long-term storage reserve for the UK grid.
The UK grid currently depends on dispatchable gas-fired generation to back up renewables, which are mainly wind. About 50% of the gas supply comes from UK North Sea production, but as production declines, the UK will be importing up to 90% of its gas needs during peak winter demand periods. So security of gas supply becomes critical for the UK’s energy security. The UK currently has very little gas storage, less than six days of national supply. The EU has around 80 days, and other big importers like China have 40-plus days. Our gas storage offers seasonal capability, and hydrogen storage is the decarbonization pathway for that gas storage.
The system is rapid response, so we can dispatch power from a cold start within a couple of minutes, and with the strategic reserve from gas and hydrogen storage, we can provide flexibility across any time frame. A battery has a response time of milliseconds to seconds, but its duration capability is about an hour and a half. Pumped hydro operates within the hour mark. We cover both of those markets, plus the strategic reserve.
When is final investment decision (FID) and when would the first cavern be operating?
The FID target is 2028 for the LDES compressed air project, and that hangs off the cap-and-floor process, which provides the sovereign guarantee on the revenue stream for project financing. We’re looking at first operations at the end of 2031 or early 2032. Compare that to alternative clean energy solutions such as pumped hydro or nuclear, which have far longer development timescales.
What concerns you most on the road to FID? What needs to be locked down in the next year or two?
We can only move as fast as policy and regulatory frameworks are rolled out. Mobilizing investment needs those government signals to build investor confidence in inward investment into the UK, so timely rollout is key.
There are two main areas of policy. One is gas security of supply. A consultation was launched at the end of last year, and we put our gas storage project forward. With 90% import dependency, the UK is highly exposed to import disruption, and the government needs to move fast to get projects such as ours up and running to shore up the country’s energy security. We expect that to be addressed in the Energy Independence Bill in the autumn.
The second is the government’s position on hydrogen. The hydrogen strategy is a long-awaited piece of government direction that will drive the next round of hydrogen investment. Our approach to hydrogen production is commercially attractive, notably because of the high-value graphite by-product of our process, but we still need the framework rolled out so investment can be mobilized.
Your last accounts carried a going-concern warning from your auditor. What needs to happen for that to go away, and how much cash do you have?
We’re a small-cap company, with a market cap of just over GBP 20 million ($26.6 million), and we’re pre-revenue, so going-concern disclosures are typical for companies like ours. Our going-concern status is a matter of securing financing for the development work we plan to do, and that’s a continual exercise. So there’s nothing particularly abnormal about it.
Is there anything else you’d like to add?
As renewables in the UK expand and wind generates surpluses, the role for batteries is very limited relative to the challenge, because of their technical limitations on duration. In a solar-dominated world, batteries have a more natural role to play. So the move to other storage technologies is absolutely critical for the UK’s energy future. It won’t be done by batteries, and storage solutions like MESH are critical to bringing down electricity bills by stopping the waste.

title: Over Easy Solar launches 256 W vertical rooftop PV unit - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Over Easy Solar’s xM-3 Quattro-256S is a 256 W vertical bifacial rooftop PV unit featuring HJT cells, 95% bifaciality and a 1,000 V maximum system voltage. Each unit covers 2.31 m², weighs 28.4 kg and has a 15-year product warranty.
Emiliano Bellini
30 Sep 2026
Research & Development
Commercial & industrial
Residential
The xM-3 QUATTRO-256S system
Vertical solar specialist
Over Easy Solar
has recently released a new version of its vertical PV system for rooftop applications.
“We have just received the Environmental Product Declaration (EPD) for our xM-3 flat-roof system,” the company’s CEO, Trygve Mongstad, told
pv magazine
. “As far as we have been able to establish, this is the first EPD globally for a rooftop PV product covering both the solar panels and the mechanical mounting structure in the same declaration.”
“One interesting detail is that the EPD is expressed per square meter of installed system rather than per kilowatt. The A1-A3 footprint is 51.5 kg CO₂e/m², including both the panels and mounting system. The equivalent global warming footprint for energy generation would be 19 g CO₂e/kWh, assuming a specific yield of 1,000 kWh/kW,” he added.
The xM-3 Quattor-256S is a 256 W bifacial PV unit designed for flat rooftops, including green and gravel roofs.
The prefabricated system consists of four
OES64-EU modules
arranged vertically. According to the manufacturer, the lightweight design allows unobstructed access for roof inspection, maintenance and repairs. The company offers different support feet for conventional flat roofs, green roofs, gravel surfaces and applications in regions with heavy snowfall.
Each xM-3 Quarttro-256S unit covers 2.31 m² of roof area and weighs approximately 28.4 kg, corresponding to an area load of around 12.2 kg/m². Depending on the support used, ground clearance ranges from 57 mm to 117 mm. The unit incorporates two 3.2 mm sheets of tempered solar glass.
The product uses silicon heterojunction (HJT) solar cells and has a bifaciality factor of 95%. It delivers 256 W at standard test conditions, with a power tolerance of around 3%. Maximum power voltage is 32.96 V and maximum power current is 7.74 A, while open-circuit voltage is 39 V and short-circuit current is 8.04 A. The maximum system voltage is 1,000 V DC.
The module has a power temperature coefficient of -0.24%/C and an operating temperature range of -40 C to 85 C.
Over Easy Solar lists a design load of 1,600 Pa, with a safety factor of 1.5, corresponding to 2,400 Pa. The junction box and connectors are rated IP68, while the product has Class II electrical protection and Class B fire safety.
The manufacturer said 27 units, representing 6.9 kWp of capacity, can be shipped on a single pallet measuring 2,070 mm × 1,600 mm × 1,255 mm.
Several mounting options are available for different rooftop applications, including the STD 60 for conventional flat roofs, the BIO 120 for green roofs, and the STD 125 for gravel roofs or locations with heavy snowfall.
The company specifies first-year power degradation of 1%, followed by annual degradation of 0.583%. The product comes with a 15-year product warranty and a 25-year power-output warranty. Its reference service life in the EPD is also 25 years.
The system is certified to IEC/EN 61215 and IEC/EN 61730 standards, among others, while the datasheet also lists UL 61730 certification. Wind-load calculations are available according to standards covering several European markets, as well as the United States, Canada, Japan and South Korea.
The product is manufactured in China, with the EPD modeling distribution to Norway.

title: Chinese scientists develop hydrogen-powered CO₂ heat pump with PCM storage - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Chinese researchers have modeled a heating system combining PEM fuel cells, a CO₂ heat pump and phase-change thermal storage, assessing the impact of different thermal boundary conditions. The results show that cathode inlet temperature has the strongest effect on hydrogen-to-heat and hydrogen-to-electricity performance, while the PCM tank can meet modeled domestic hot water demand.
Lior Kahana
30 Sep 2026
Research & Development
Heat pumps
Hydrogen
Schematic of the system
A research group in China has simulated the operation of a heating system combining a hydrogen fuel cell, a CO₂ heat pump and phase-change thermal storage. The study examined how ambient temperature and the fuel cell’s anode and cathode inlet temperatures affect hydrogen consumption, heat storage and system efficiency.
“Until now, the integration of a proton exchange membrane fuel cell (PEMFC)-driven CO₂ heat pump with a phase change material (PCM) tank has not been systematically investigated,” the researchers said. “In addition, the extent to which thermal boundary conditions influence the hydrogen-to-electricity-to-heat conversion pathway has remained insufficiently understood.”
The simulated system comprises 30 PEMFC stacks, each containing 20 cells, which supply electricity directly to the CO₂ heat pump compressor. The compressor adjusts its speed according to the fuel cells’ power output and sends hot CO₂ to a gas cooler, where it heats water circulating through the thermal storage tank at a flow rate of 0.08 kg/s.
The tank contains 100 hexadecane-filled tubes, each measuring 0.4 m in length and 0.05 m in diameter. Hexadecane is a PCM that absorbs heat as it melts at 18 C. After leaving the gas cooler, the CO₂ passes through an expansion valve and then an evaporator, where it extracts heat from either air or water at 19 C. A suction accumulator and internal heat exchanger help prevent liquid CO₂ from entering the compressor, completing the cycle.
The researchers conducted the simulations in MATLAB. They individually varied the ambient temperature around the fuel cell and the anode and cathode inlet temperatures from 2 C to 34 C, while holding the other two parameters at 25 C. The air and water heat sources were maintained at 19 C, while the water and PCM in the storage tank were initially set at 5 C. Each simulation ended when the gas cooler outlet water temperature reached 30 C.
“The results indicated that, compared with ambient temperature and anode inlet temperature, cathode inlet temperature exerted a stronger influence on the system performance indicators,” the researchers said.
They also noted that, as the cathode inlet temperature increased from 2 C to 34 C, the hydrogen-to-heat factor rose by 29.4%, from 28.458 kWh/kg to 36.825 kWh/kg, while the hydrogen-to-electricity factor increased by 60.97%, from 8.825 kWh/kg to 14.206 kWh/kg. Meanwhile, the system coefficient of performance (COP) fell by 19.63%, from 3.225 to 2.592.
For a target daily domestic hot water demand of 75 liters and a temperature increase of 40 C, the researchers estimated that the PCM tank would need to supply about 3.5 kWh of thermal energy. “As a result, the PCM tank proved capable of meeting the hot water demand,” they said.
The findings are presented in the study “
Impact of thermal boundary conditions on hydrogen-driven CO₂ heat pump with PCM
,” published in
Results in Engineering
. Scientists from China’s
Dongguan University of Technology
Sun Yat-sen University
contributed to the research.

title: Fox ESS launches modular C&I battery system scalable to 96 MWh - pv magazine Global
content:
Technology & Products
Fox ESS’s Power Beast pairs a 125 kW hybrid inverter with stackable lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery modules for commercial and industrial (C&I) users, as the Chinese company awaits approval for a Shenzhen stock listing.
Brian Publicover
30 Sep 2026
Technology & Products
Batteries
Commercial & industrial
Energy Storage
Chinese inverter and battery maker Fox ESS has unveiled a modular C&I storage system that it says can scale from 28 kWh to nearly 1,000 kWh on a single inverter. The company lists a maximum on-grid configuration of 100 units in parallel, for 96 MWh, and an off-grid maximum of 30 units, for 28.8 MWh.
The system, called Power Beast, was launched on last week at a company event in Wenzhou, China. It combines Fox ESS’s 125 kW H3 Plus hybrid inverter with its CQ series of high-voltage batteries.
According to the inverter’s datasheet, it has a battery voltage range of 180 V to 950 V, a maximum efficiency of 98.5% and an IP65 rating. The datasheets for the 5.99 kWh CQ6 and 7.02 kWh CQ7 modules list certification to IEC 62619 and a cycle life of at least 6,000 cycles to 70% state of health.
Fox ESS has not published a datasheet for the larger CQ20 module, which it says achieves 7 kg per kWh at module level, or about 143 Wh/kg. The company describes the CQ20 as “the industry’s first modular C&I energy storage system with a fully integrated hybrid inverter.” Sigenergy has offered a similar architecture since launching its
SigenStack
at Intersolar Europe in June 2024. The system pairs a hybrid inverter of up to 125 kW with stackable battery modules.
Fox ESS said the modular design cuts total installation time by 90%, without specifying the baseline. At the launch, a team assembled and connected a 316 kWh system in under 30 minutes, the company said.
Fox ESS did not disclose pricing, launch markets, delivery dates, warranty terms, system-level certifications or its cell supplier.
The launch comes as Fox ESS, which is registered in China as Maitian Energy, pursues a listing on the Shenzhen Stock Exchange’s ChiNext board, where it plans to raise CNY 1.66 billion ($247.6 million). Its prospectus reports 2025 revenue of CNY 6.53 billion and net profit of CNY 1.12 billion, with more than 99% of its main-business revenue earned outside China.

title: EU’s largest solar project reaches financial close - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
The €561 million ($637.3 million) financing package allows Rezolv Energy’s 1.3 GW solar project, to be built in western Romania, to move into construction.
Patrick Jowett
30 Sep 2026
Applications & Installations
Highlights
Utility-scale
Rezolv Energy’s 225 MW St. George solar park in Bulgaria was switched on earlier this year.
Prague-headquartered independent power producer Rezolv Energy says it has signed an up to €561 million ($637.3 million) financing package for its planned 1.3 GW solar plant.
According to an update posted by Rezolv on LinkedIn, the Dama solar project, to be built in the Arad county of western Romania, will be the largest onshore renewable energy project in the European Union.
It is expected to generate around 1.8 TWh of electricity annually once fully operational, equivalent to around 36% of Romania’s total solar electricity generation last year. Rezlov says its production will cover the consumption of over 280,000 households, or close to one million people.
The financing package is underpinned by an anchor investment by the European Investment Bank and comes from a consortium of 14 lenders including ten commercial banks alongside the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development, International Finance Corporation and Black Sea Trade & Development Bank.
Rezolv adds that the financing is its largest transaction signed to date. It is underpinned by two contracts for difference awarded to the project during Romania’s
second renewables auction
covering 520 MW of the total capacity, the company added, alongside an additional corporate power purchase agreement with an unnamed offtaker.
The financial close follows the granting of final legal approvals for the project by the Romanian Energy Regulatory Authority last month.
Rezolv says the project will now move into construction with commercial operations expected in the second half of 2028.
Romania’s solar market has continued to
develop strongly
this year, with cumulative capacity
exceeding 8.5 GW
as of the end of July.

title: Belgium reveals results of PV cable assessment - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
Belgian authorities found that nine of 10 PV cables tested achieved a lower fire-reaction class than their manufacturers had declared. However, the manufacturers provided additional accredited laboratory tests supporting their declarations, prompting the authorities to close the cases without further action.
Emiliano Bellini
30 Sep 2026
Applications & Installations
Belgium’s Federal Public Service (FPS) Economy, the country’s market surveillance authority, published last week the
of a PV cable inspection and testing campaign conducted in 2024.
The authority said the campaign had two objectives: to verify compliance with the requirements of Regulation (EU) No. 305/2011 and to prevent unfair competition.
“As part of the sampling and testing campaign, PV cable samples were collected for laboratory analysis,” FPS Economy said. “The tests were intended to determine whether the performance characteristics reported by manufacturers in their Declarations of Performance (DoPs) corresponded with results obtained by a notified body.”
Testing was carried out by Belgium’s Scientific Institute of Public Service (ISSeP), an accredited laboratory.
The assessment covered PV cables from 10 undisclosed manufacturers. Five cables had a cross-section of 4 mm² and five had a cross-section of 6 mm².
An initial administrative compliance check found that all 10 cables carried CE markings and were accompanied by DoPs, with no significant documentation issues identified.
The cables were then subjected to reaction-to-fire testing under applicable European standards. Under the European classification system for electrical cables, Cca and Dca indicate different levels of contribution to the development and spread of fire, with Cca representing better fire performance than Dca.
Laboratory testing revealed significant discrepancies between declared and measured performance. Only one of the 10 cables achieved the Cca reaction-to-fire class declared by its manufacturer. The remaining nine were classified as Dca in the ISSeP tests, despite manufacturers declaring them as Cca.
FPS Economy subsequently contacted the manufacturers of the nine cables and asked them to provide evidence supporting their declared classifications. The manufacturers submitted additional test reports from accredited notified laboratories based on samples from the same production batches.
“Those results supported the manufacturers’ declared fire classifications,” the authority said. “Consequently, FPS Economy decided not to pursue the cases further.”

title: Ireland introduces €600 residential battery grant, expands PV support - pv magazine Global
content:

Irish householders will be able to avail of a €600 battery grant as part of a package of renewable energy supports effective from October 6. Grants of up to €9,000 for lower-income householders to install solar and batteries will also be included as well as support for businesses.
Blathnaid O’Dea
30 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Residential energy
Ireland has approved a new package of energy grants for homes and businesses, effective Oct. 6.
The measures include enhanced support for solar PV, alongside incentives for home heating decarbonization and energy retrofits. A new residential battery grant worth up to €600 ($681) is also being introduced.
Ireland already offers a state-administered grant of up to €1,800 for homeowners installing residential solar panels. From Oct. 6, eligibility will be expanded to include newer homes built and occupied before 2025.
Grants of up to €9,000 will also be introduced for lower-income households installing solar and battery systems, while solar-plus-storage systems will be fully funded for people classed as medically vulnerable. In both cases, funding will cover battery capacities of up to 5 kWh and PV systems of up to 4 kW.
The package also includes a €2,000 grant to encourage households to replace boilers with heat pumps.
Solar Ireland, which represents the country’s solar sector, welcomed the introduction of the residential battery grant.
“We have long called for the reintroduction of support for residential battery storage,” said Solar Ireland CEO Ronan Power. “Batteries allow households to make better use of the solar electricity they generate, reduce reliance on the grid during peak periods and provide greater protection from future energy price volatility.”
The package also includes expanded support for businesses. The Irish government said businesses accessing the enhanced solar PV support could reduce annual energy costs by up to €300,000. Grants for solar thermal systems and heat pumps could also deliver savings of up to 45%.
“Businesses across Ireland are facing significant challenges from high energy costs, and we know that improving competitiveness means helping firms reduce their overheads wherever possible,” said Irish Minister for Enterprise, Tourism and Employment Peter Burke.
William Walsh, CEO of the Sustainable Energy Authority of Ireland (SEAI), the state agency administering the grants, said the organization has recorded a 200% increase in applications for some grants.
“We’ve had
unprecedented demand
to our programs this year. These new measures are really welcome and will help us reach even more people next year, especially those most in need,” Walsh said.
The measures come ahead of the Irish government’s 2027 budget, which is due to be announced in the coming weeks. Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment Darragh O’Brien said further measures will be considered as part of next year’s budget.
“The government has already introduced more than €1.4 billion in energy affordability measures since March,” he said.

title: Researchers test laminated bamboo structures for floating PV platforms - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Chinese researchers tested thin-plate glued laminated bamboo (glubam) assemblies for use in floating PV platforms, assessing their flexural behavior under different plate and bolt configurations. The results show that plate configuration, bolt spacing, bolt diameter, and thickness distribution can significantly affect the structures’ ultimate load capacity.
Lior Kahana
30 Sep 2026
Research & Development
Commercial & industrial
Utility-scale
Illustration of the proposed system
A research team in China has analyzed the flexural behavior of thin-plate glued laminated bamboo (glubam) systems for floating PV platforms.
“Glubam systems show promising potential for FPV platforms due to their high strength-to-weight ratio, low carbon footprint, and favorable balance between flexibility and bending stiffness,” the researchers said. “This study investigates the flexural behavior of bolted three-layer thin-plate glubam assemblies for floating photovoltaic structures under monotonic loading.”
The researchers tested different glubam assemblies using four-point bending tests with varying plate configurations and thicknesses, alongside numerical simulations and parametric analyses. They also developed mechanics-based models for bending stiffness and ultimate capacity.
For the experimental part of the study, the researchers built six glubam configurations and tested two specimens of each. All specimens were 200 mm wide and featured continuous 2,000 mm upper and lower plates, a 15 mm segmented middle plate, a 10 mm lower plate, and M10 bolts. To create the six configurations, they combined two upper-plate thicknesses – 20 mm and 25 mm – with three middle-layer layouts: 1,200 + 1,200 mm, 600 + 600 + 600 mm, and 600 + 600 + 600 + 600 mm.
The researchers subjected the specimens to four-point bending tests. The specimens rested on supports spaced 1,500 mm apart, with loads applied at two points 700 mm apart.
The team recorded load, midspan deflection, and plate strain as the specimens approached their peak loads. It then developed ABAQUS models of the six configurations and compared the predicted stiffness and peak loads with the experimental results.
The scientists subsequently used the models to assess how bolt diameter, bolt spacing, and plate thickness affected load-bearing capacity.
“The flexural failure of the assemblies was governed by rolling shear of the middle layer, followed by cracking of the upper plate,” they said. “The flexural stiffness showed limited sensitivity to middle-layer segment length and configuration within the investigated range, whereas the ultimate capacity depended on whether a middle-layer discontinuity was located within the shear span.”
Compared with the 1,200 + 1,200 mm layout, the 600 + 600 + 600 + 600 mm configuration reduced ultimate load capacity by 10.00% with the 25 mm upper plate and by 28.22% with the 20 mm upper plate. For the 600 + 600 + 600 mm configuration, the corresponding reductions were limited to 6.22% and 2.49%, respectively.
The parametric analysis showed that increasing bolt diameter from 10 mm to 12 mm improved ultimate moment capacity by between 8.43% and 12.11%, although the benefit diminished at larger diameters. Reducing bolt spacing from 200 mm to 100 mm was more effective, increasing capacity by 40.39%, provided that minimum spacing and edge-distance requirements were met.
“Increasing upper-plate thickness from 15 mm to 20 mm increased capacity by 20.54%, whereas a further increase from 25 mm to 30 mm raised capacity by only 3.19%,” the researchers said. “At a fixed total thickness, allocating additional thickness to the face plates, particularly the lower plate, produced a greater increase in ultimate capacity than allocating it to the middle plate.”
The study,
“Flexural behavior of three-layer thin-plate glubam assemblies for floating photovoltaic platforms”
, was published in
Structures
. Researchers from China’s
Hebei University of Engineering
Tianjin University
Tianjin University of Technology
Hong Kong Polytechnic University
contributed to the work.

title: Panasonic deploys fuel cell, heat pump at PV-powered hydrogen house - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Panasonic has deployed a 10 kW pure hydrogen fuel cell and a 9 kW air-to-water heat pump at Finland’s Hydrogen House, which features rooftop PV and up to 90 kg of hydrogen storage. The integrated system uses solar-generated hydrogen to provide electricity, space heating and hot water, while also recovering waste heat from the fuel cell.
Emiliano Bellini
30 Sep 2026
Research & Development
Energy Storage
Heat pumps
Hydrogen
Residential
Hydrogen House operated by Cefmof in Central Finland
Japanese electronics manufacturer
Panasonic
has started operating a fuel cell system and an air-to-water heat pump at the Hydrogen House, a demonstration facility run by the Central Finland Mobility Foundation (Cefmof) in Jyväskylä, central Finland.
Panasonic said the project is testing an integrated energy system combining its
Pure Hydrogen Fuel Cell technology
Aquarea air-to-water heat pump
. The system supplies electricity to the building and thermal energy for space heating, with the aim of improving overall energy efficiency and optimizing hydrogen consumption.
The company said limited daylight hours in central Finland during winter make it difficult to rely on solar generation throughout the year. The demonstration will therefore assess the performance and scalability of the combined fuel cell and heat pump system under local conditions.
The Hydrogen House combines rooftop PV with hydrogen production and storage. Electricity from the solar array powers an electrolyzer that produces hydrogen, which is stored in tanks with a total capacity of up to 90 kg and distributed across the property through an underground pipeline.
The stored hydrogen supplies several applications, including a fireplace, oven, grill and sauna. When PV generation is insufficient, the fuel cell converts hydrogen into electricity. The system also recovers waste heat from the fuel cell for thermal applications.
Overview of the integrated hydrogen energy and heat pump solution
The heat pump provides the house’s main space heating and hot water, using electricity from the PV system or, when solar generation is insufficient, electricity produced by the hydrogen fuel cell.
“At full capacity, the Pure Hydrogen Fuel Cell delivers 10 kW of electrical output, while the air-to-water heat pump provides 9 kW of thermal output,” Panasonic said, without providing further technical details about the system.
“This project is thought to be one of the first integrated hydrogen energy demonstrations in Europe, comparable to existing projects in Japan,” it added. “It is expected to provide valuable insights into the feasibility of indoor hydrogen energy systems and their integration with heating equipment under Finland’s harsh winter conditions.”
Panasonic launched its
H2 Kibou pure hydrogen fuel cell system
in 2021. The original 5 kW unit uses hydrogen with a purity of more than 99.97% and has an electrical efficiency of 56%. Panasonic said heat recovery can increase the system’s overall energy efficiency to as much as 95%.
Panasonic has also deployed the technology in systems combining hydrogen fuel cells, solar PV and battery storage. In 2022, it commissioned a
demonstration facility at its fuel cell factory in Kusatsu, Japan
, featuring 99 H2 Kibou units with a combined capacity of 495 kW, alongside a 570 kW PV array and 1.1 MWh of battery storage. Panasonic later deployed a similar configuration at its
microwave oven factory in Cardiff, Wales
, combining 21 5 kW hydrogen fuel cell generators with 372 kW of PV and 1 MWh of battery storage.
Panasonic has marketed its
Aquarea air-to-water heat pumps
in Europe since 2008. The systems provide space heating and domestic hot water by extracting heat from ambient air. The company has expanded the Aquarea range over the years, including models that use propane (R290) as a refrigerant.
Panasonic subsequently introduced its
Aquarea L series
for residential applications. The R290 units have heating capacities ranging from 5 kW to 8 kW and can supply hot water at temperatures of up to 75 C. They are also smart-grid ready for integration with rooftop PV systems.
In July 2025, Panasonic further expanded its R290 portfolio with the launch of the
Aquarea DHW Heat Pump
, a dedicated domestic hot water solution. The system uses ambient air as an additional energy source and is available in both wall-mounted and floor-standing configurations.

title: Cuba's PV capacity tops 1.4 GW - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Cuba has installed 1.42 GW of solar capacity across 144 photovoltaic plants and expects to exceed 1.5 GW by the end of 2026. Renewables now account for 21.4% of electricity generation, while the country is also expanding energy storage and solar-powered water pumping.
Luis Ini
30 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Americas
A PV system operating in Cuba
Cuba has reached 1.42 GW of installed solar capacity across 144 photovoltaic plants and expects the total to exceed 1.5 GW by the end of 2026, according to Cuban President Miguel Díaz-Canel.
Speaking on the radio program
Criterio Compartido
, broadcast from the Radio Rebelde studios, Díaz-Canel said Cuba has installed 1,418 MW of solar capacity across 144 projects.
“We expect to close the year with more than 1,500 MW,” he said while discussing the country’s energy transition.
Díaz-Canel said more than 563 MW of additional generation capacity has been installed at consumer sites in the state and non-state sectors. He said deployment is growing fastest in the private sector, where on-site solar generation now covers around 20% of electricity consumption, reducing demand on Cuba’s National Electric Power System (SEN).
Renewable energy sources currently account for 21.4% of Cuba’s electricity generation, according to Díaz-Canel.
He also provided figures for the country’s energy storage rollout, saying 50 MW of storage capacity has been installed and another 100 MW is scheduled to come online in October.
Solar deployment is also expanding into water pumping. Díaz-Canel said 646 solar-powered pumps have been installed for public water supplies, while more than 1,000 units have been deployed for livestock and irrigation. Seven provinces have also launched initiatives based on distributed generation systems and solar plants.
The government plans to deploy another 200 MW of solar capacity specifically for water pumping. Díaz-Canel said the aim is to make pumping operations independent of the SEN in the first months of 2027, before extending the initiative to the remaining provinces.
Renewables are also being deployed across public services. According to figures presented by Díaz-Canel, renewable energy systems are in use at 99% of polyclinics, 47% of hospitals, 89% of nursing homes and elderly day-care centers, 99% of maternity homes, 98% of funeral homes, 16% of homes for children without parental care, and 72% of banks.
In the communications sector, 97% of radio stations have photovoltaic systems, along with 25% of Radio Cuba transmitters and 25% of Etecsa base stations, Díaz-Canel said.
He added that Cuban banks offer financing for renewable energy installations to individuals and businesses. Cuba has also established a feed-in tariff of CUP 90 ($0.37) per kWh for electricity supplied to the SEN and expanded tax incentives for renewable energy installations.

title: New home wallpaper absorbs humidity from air to generate power for devices
content: Rooftop solar panels have officially hit the mainstream, topping over 6 million American homes. But your roof is no longer the only domestic real estate eyeing a green energy makeover.What if your living room walls could harvest electricity from thin air? Researchers at Binghamton University have unveiled a paper-based, energy-harvesting “wallpaper” that converts indoor humidity into real electric current. “We put a lot of energy into HVAC systems to remove moisture from the air, but if we use this concept, we could reduce or control moisture levels while also generating electricity,” said Professor Seokheun “Sean” Choi, a faculty member at the Thomas J. Watson College of Engineering and Applied Science’s Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering. Powered by moistureThe wallpaper technology depends on tiny moist-electric generators (MEGs). These microscopic powerhouses draw ambient water vapor from the air. Once trapped, the moisture forces ions inside the material to separate, creating a natural concentration gradient. That subtle shift creates a steady voltage between the front and back of the paper, and interestingly, no sunlight is required. Engineers have played with moisture-harvesting tech before, but previous designs focused almost exclusively on the unpredictable outdoors. Rainstorms can cause power to spike, while blistering sun can kill it completely.On the other hand, indoor air is a stable environment. Most homes stay between 30 percent and 60 percent humidity year-round. Better yet, everyday human life constantly recharges the system. Cooking dinner, taking a hot shower, or simply breathing out fills the room with untapped potential. To make the tech cheap, functional, and attractive, the team drew on “papertronics” — the art of printing electronic circuits directly onto paper. The layout works like a miniature circuit board. Glycerol applied along the outer edges acts as a sponge, snatching water molecules from the surrounding room. At the center sits a raised polymer layer patterned with wax. This central structure carefully controls how water evaporates, maintaining a directional flow of moisture across the sheet to keep electricity flowing continuously. Wallpaper to run IoT devicesThe researchers demonstrated the design’s practical power by building a full-scale wallpaper sheet with 1,596 interconnected units. A single unit produces roughly 0.34 V with a power density of 2.2 µW/cm² at 80 percent relative humidity. This large-scale array generated enough continuous electricity to power a wireless keyboard without any batteries.Beyond power, the array dropped indoor humidity in a test space from 38 percent down to 32 percent, proving its dual role as a passive dehumidifier. Nobody wants a living room wall crisscrossed with messy wires. To fix the aesthetic problem, the researchers routed every connection behind the wallpaper. You will not power a refrigerator with paper walls, at least not anytime soon. These sheets yield modest microwatt-level power, designed specifically for low-draw devices. Think smart thermostats, ambient temperature sensors, indoor climate monitors, and wireless keyboards. Instead of swapping out toxic batteries every few months, the growing constellation of Internet-of-Things (IoT) gizmos in modern homes could simply run off the walls.Homeowners could generate clean energy and ease the strain on their air conditioners by letting the walls do some of the work. Should Choi’s vision reach mass production, the next frontier of home energy efficiency could soon be hanging right on your walls.The findings were published in the journal Advanced Energy.

title: US turns waste carbon into 2.5 barrels of synthetic jet fuel per day
content: A climate technology company has successfully produced synthetic aviation fuel from landfill-derived renewable natural gas (RNG) and captured industrial carbon dioxide (CO2) with its Aurora technology platform.The fuel was produced on a fully integrated demonstration line equipped with the 2.5-barrel-per-day Aurora Tri-Converter and Aurora Upgrader units. These were linked to an existing Fischer-Tropsch reactor run by Research Triangle Park (RTI).Aether Fuels, which is based in the US and Singapore, said that the demonstration covered the whole production process. It reportedly transformed waste-derived gaseous feedstocks into fully upgraded synthetic liquid jet fuel.Independent testing firm AmSpec confirmed that samples produced during the demo met the applicable ASTM specifications for Fischer-Tropsch Synthesized Paraffinic Kerosene (FT-SPK). “This is exciting progress for Aether as we march forward towards commercial deployment,” Conor Madigan, Aether Fuels CEO and co-founder, said. Jet fuel passes key testThe demo used mass-balanced renewable natural gas from landfill gas generated in Kentucky alongside captured industrial CO2. The company is believed to be the first in North America to produce ASTM-spec synthetic aviation fuel from mass-balanced RNG and captured industrial CO2 at this scale. As per Aether Fuels, the fuel complied with ASTM D7566 requirements applicable to FT-SPK. Under the ASTM D7566 standard, qualifying synthetic fuel can be blended with conventional kerosene at concentrations of up to 50 percent.Moreover, the blend requires no modifications to aircraft fuel tanks, pipelines, or airport fueling systems. Because the FT-SPK production route is already covered under ASTM D7566, the firm said its fuel does not require the establishment of a new ASTM pathway.“This demonstration proves Aether’s ability to scale up our integrated Aurora platform, take a feedstock through the complete end-to-end process, and produce on-spec synthetic aviation fuel,” Dhaval Shah, Aether Fuels CTO, said. “It is the culmination of over a year of hard work by Aether’s R&D team and is a tremendous milestone,” Shah continued, adding that the data collected during the demo is set to cut the technical risks associated with the firm’s next project.New fuel plant plannedThe achievement followed after an earlier Tri-Converter test with GTI Energy. The company now plans to develop Project Beacon, a commercial facility in Singapore with an annual production capacity of 2,000 metric tons. Set to produce around 50 barrels of fuel per day, the plant will have about 20 times the capacity of the latest demonstration equipment.“This is a significant achievement and puts us on the right track to successfully build and operate Project Beacon and the commercial projects that will follow,” Madigan said in a press release.Aether Fuels said larger projects are expected to produce ASTM D7566-compliant sustainable aviation fuel. This could reduce lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by more than 70 percent compared with conventional jet fuel.“We started by systematically demonstrating each part of the Aurora platform at the pilot scale, then scaled our novel technology up more than 50X in standalone demo units, and in this most recent demonstration, brought these demo units together in an integrated line that produces ASTM spec jet fuel,” Madigan concluded.
