title: Oura, World Labs Show Divergence in VC Exits
content: It’s turning out to be a great year for venture exits—as long as you’re talking about M&A. Take Monday’s news that Advanced Micro Devices would purchase Fei-Fei Li’s World Labs. The $8.2 billion all-stock purchase of the two-year-old AI startup adds to the growing list of such deals this year, which include SpaceX’s purchase of Cursor, Nvidia’s purchase of Hugging Face and Stripe’s acquisition of OpenRouter . The sale is also another win for Martin Casado’s infrastructure team at Andreessen Horowitz, which was World Labs’ largest shareholder and owns nearly 14% of the company, I reported . An expected IPO gusher, on the other hand, is at serious risk of turning into a drought. On Tuesday, health-tracking wearable company Oura said it was delaying its IPO , previously expected to take place later this week, blaming “market uncertainty.” There are definitely signs of uncertainty: The Federal Reserve just hiked rates to counter inflation; mortgage rates have topped 7%; and average gas prices have sprinted past $6 a gallon in states like California. Then there are some Silicon Valley factors. A lawyer who works with venture firms and startups told me today that AI leaders’ constant sounding of alarm bells on safety are also contributing to the market uncertainty. But investors tell us that Oura’s decision may be more particular to how it structured its listing. One of Oura’s major investors, Forerunner Ventures, intended to fully exit its position—a roughly 9% stake—at the IPO, according to its filings. The intended sale, of over 28 million of shares worth about $1.2 billion at the midpoint of the proposed IPO price range, spooked potential investors in the IPO, who saw the sale as a bearish sign, our sources tell us. Indeed, no major shareholders sold when Cerebras listed at a $56 billion valuation in its IPO earlier this year. And major SpaceX shareholders like Valor Equity Partners and DFJ Growth also held onto all of their shares in the June offering. Forerunner, known as a premier consumer investor before the AI boom, took its lumps when companies like makeup brand Glossier lost their sheen. It raised a $500 million fund, its seventh, in November 2024 and has since invested in AI companies like voice dictation company Wispr Flow and assistant startup Town. It’s not clear why Forerunner intended to sell its stake in Oura at the IPO. A representative from the firm didn’t respond to requests for comment. But Forerunner’s planned sale wasn’t the only warning sign. The target valuation was too high for some prospective IPO investors, people familiar with the discussion said. As Martin wrote earlier this week , the mid-point of Oura’s expected $40 to $44 pricing range looked to value the company at nine times this year’s estimated revenue. That was much higher than other niche hardware makers like Sonos and about on par with the far more diversified Apple. Unhelpfully, Wall Street analysts had started to draw comparisons between Oura and GoPro, the action-camera maker that skirted insolvency earlier this year. To be fair, Oura isn’t under the gun to go public: It reported $60.8 million in net profit on $1.2 billion in revenue in the nine months ended June, though it posted a loss in the June quarter. Most of what it would have raised in the IPO would go to satisfy tax payments related to employee stock awards. Delaying its IPO could give Oura time to reconsider how much existing shareholders will sell in the offering, the person who has spoken to the company’s executives said. Oura could possibly still go public in the fourth quarter of this year—closer to the holiday season, when good tidings (and sales) may relieve the fall gloom. — Valida Pau contributed to this report. title: Oura’s IPO Delay Signals Broader Market Stall
content: The IPO market appears to have stalled, which could be a problem for Anthropic. Fitness ring maker Oura’s postponement of its IPO on Tuesday, citing “uncertainty in the IPO market,” followed similar moves by metals producer Amaero last week and Holtec Nuclear Corp. the week before that. Then there’s SB Energy, the SoftBank-controlled power developer for data centers, which made public its IPO paperwork on Sept. 1 (two days before Oura did so) but hasn’t yet begun to market the offering. You don’t have to be a rocket scientist to figure out what’s going on. In its statement explaining its IPO postponement two weeks ago, Holtec mentioned “headwinds” including rising energy costs, trade tensions, military conflicts and rising interest rates. In short, it’s the world we live in. On top of that, Holtec—which sells to data centers—cited “uncertainty over data center development.” To be sure, companies with a risky story or overhigh valuation face a particularly tough time going public in a troubled market like this one. Oura, which claimed to be seeing “strong demand” from investors, had proposed a pricing range that implied a valuation arguably twice as high as it should have been. ( Bloomberg reported Tuesday the valuation caused some investors to push back.) And as we pointed out on Sunday , Oura reminded some on Wall Street of other single-product hardware firms that had not done well. SB Energy is in a different situation, one closer to that of Nscale which has also filed to go public. Both have ambitions to become major AI data center operators but are still very early in their development. As we pointed out in this piece , SB Energy doesn’t yet have any data centers in operation. Nscale‘s business isn’t quite as embryonic but as we outlined in this analysis on Tuesday , Nscale has to persuade investors of its ability to raise financing for the data centers it needs to build. A person with knowledge of the situation tells me Nscale is moving forward with the IPO process. While that may be true, I wouldn’t be surprised if we wake up someday soon to see the news that Nscale has decided to postpone. What does all this mean for Anthropic, which had been expected to go public sometime soon, in hopes of raising close to $100 billion? A choppy market could complicate those aspirations. Moreover, the leak to Reuters on Monday night of Anthropic’s confidential IPO prospectus highlights the risks for the company. Anthropic, according to Reuters, warns in the filing that AI poses “existential risks to humanity.” It also details the financial risks. We already know debt investors are getting more picky about financing data centers and chips, which could complicate the data center build-out so important to Anthropic’s growth. All in all, the question now may be not whether Anthropic delays its IPO, but when. OpenAI Give New Meaning to Dots OpenAI responded to Meta Platforms’ Muse personal assistant with its own line of AI assistants—with the unfortunate name of Dots. In a livestreamed presentation, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and other staffers outlined how paying ChatGPT users could use Dots to do everything from booking restaurant reservations to helping with detailed work-related processes. Unfortunately, Elon Musk’s SpaceX has the jump on OpenAI. My colleague Grace Kay tells me AI coding firm Cursor was thinking of using Dot (singular) as the name of its personal assistant before SpaceX acquired Cursor. After that, SpaceX abandoned the Dot name in favor of Grok Bot. But SpaceX doesn’t seem to have given up the name dot.com . If you type that into your web browser, you get directed to a page about Grok Bot . ( Dots.com appears to be a clothing site). Given the acrimonious history between Musk and Altman, don't expect the SpaceX CEO to give up the web address to his foe, OpenAI. title: Google Is Paying About 100 Digital Publishers for AI Overviews
content: Google has been paying roughly 100 digital publishers for how much their content contributes to AI-powered answers to search and other products, according to people familiar with tests. The pilot program signals a further shift by the company toward paying publishers for content that shows up in its powerful search engine. Google has historically taken the attitude that it shouldn’t pay publishers whose content answers users’ queries, on the grounds that the questions direct traffic to their websites. But the advent of AI-powered summaries, called AI Overviews, has drastically reduced the amount of traffic Google’s search refers to websites, prompting widespread complaints about Google, including lawsuits from some publishers. The program is unlikely to silence those complaints, however. For several small to midsize blogs and websites testing the programs, the payments amount to less than one-tenth of 1% of their advertising revenue, according to people familiar with the payouts. The small scale of the payouts has deterred some larger ones from using the program, three people familiar with the matter said. By holding out, they hope to pressure Google and others to pay more for content used by AI. Other publishers see the latest program as a chance to learn what content Google’s AI values and adapt theirs to match. An executive at one participating publisher said Google appears to be testing a new deal in which it uses publishers’ content and decides for itself what that content is worth. Google started testing the program involving its AI Overviews, AI Mode and Gemini chatbot less than a year ago, according to a person close to Google. Payments have varied widely. One publisher that joined a few months ago has earned about $50,000 to $60,000 so far, which doesn’t represent that much of its business, the publisher said. Another that joined early on is earning more than $1 million a year, which represents a bigger slice of its revenue, according to people familiar with the program. Smaller sites have earned less than $1,000 over several months, according to those people. Publishers can track how often their content is used and how much they’re paid through Google Search Console, a tool that helps them measure and monitor the website’s performance and search traffic. If enough publishers stick with it, the program could represent a model for how other AI companies handle websites whose content feeds their models’ answers. Digiday first reported on the existence of the program but hasn’t reported on the payment amounts, the number of publishers in the program and other details. Publisher Complaints Google’s attitude to paying publishers has evolved over time. After resisting paying news publishers for content that showed in some products for many years, and under pressure from regulators and lawmakers internationally, it has increasingly struck licensing and partnership agreements to pay publishers. Things changed again when tech firms began training AI models. For a time, Google was slow to pay publishers for using their models in AI, although it inked a deal in 2024 to license Reddit’s data for training its Gemini model. Then in January 2025, Google also struck a deal with the Associated Press to provide a real-time news feed to the Gemini app. The program, which includes more than 200 publications globally, is also testing audio briefings for those who prefer listening. And in recent months, it started a program to pay publishers such as The Washington Post and The Guardian to make their content more visible in AI-powered article overviews in Google News. The AI Overviews program follows complaints by publishers that the emergence of Google AI products summarizing web answers has reduced the need for people to visit their websites. World History Encyclopedia, an online reference site that isn’t part of the pilot, says its Google traffic has fallen 25% to 35% in each of the past two years across its site, and is down about 50% from 2024. Pages with an AI Overview were hit hardest, said Jan van der Crabben, World History Encyclopedia founder. Google, like other model makers, needs these web publishers to stay active. Google models trained on internet content lose their relevancy after a while. To keep its answers current and accurate, the model checks them against content it finds in Google’s search and revises them to reduce hallucinations, when the model confidently produces an answer that is plainly wrong. Not every source counts equally under the program. For example, if the model consulted 100 websites for an answer, perhaps only five, or 5%, would meaningfully improve that response. Some participants said they still don’t know how their payments are calculated, including what counts as a meaningful contribution or which kinds of content are valued most, and said payments can change from month to month without explanation. Patterns are starting to emerge, however. Content on topics that are less widely covered online but draw strong user interest, such as anime and gaming, appear to earn more, according to people familiar with the discussions. The experiment is running as regulators step up pressure on Google over how it uses publishers’ content. Penske Media sued Google twice in four months: first in September 2025 , alleging that AI Overviews siphoned traffic and cut its affiliate revenue while illegally tying AI Overviews inclusion to search indexing, and again in January , seeking damages off the federal court’s finding that Google illegally monopolized ad tech and thereby depressed the prices Penske could charge for ads. Under Google’s policy at the time, publishers could control some specific use of their content but couldn’t opt out while preserving their visibility in Google’s search. Google rejected both those allegations, including by arguing that publishers can block Google from indexing their sites and that advertisers and publishers have alternatives to its ad products but chose Google because it’s more affordable. In June, U.K. regulators ordered Google to let publishers opt out of its AI search features without hurting their ranking in regular search results. The European Commission separately opened an antitrust investigation in December 2025 into whether Google imposes unfair terms on publishers by using their content for its AI features without proper compensation or a real option to refuse. In response to the pressure from the U.K. and Europe, in August Google completed the opt-out option for publishers that allows them to refuse the use of their content in AI Overviews, AI Mode or Google Discover without losing visibility in search.

title: How Investors Are Financing On-Site Power to Break AI Bottlenecks
content: Companies building and operating data centers are hungry for ways to secure the power needed to move ahead with massive AI build-outs. That’s prompted big financing pledges and creative dealmaking for on-site power that can cut data centers’ reliance on electric grids. Investors are getting in on the crunch through several angles, including large investments in specific projects, such as new on-site power plants. Some investors are also taking equity stakes in companies that provide on-site power, or providing outside capital to finance equipment like fuel cells for end customers such as AI cloud providers. A Blackstone-led group, including KKR and Apollo, this summer agreed to invest $5.3 billion for a 49% stake in five gas-fired power projects pipeline giant Williams is developing to supply on-site power for data centers. Of the $5.3 billion, $4.4 billion will cover the investors’ share of expected project costs, Williams said. Though on-site power can be pricier than connecting to the grid, availability and speed is an obvious advantage. Williams, which recently expanded into developing and running on-site generation for data centers, said last month it brought its first 200 megawatts online less than 18 months after commercialization. By comparison, Fitch Ratings estimates that building new infrastructure such as grid-connected power plants and high-voltage transmission lines can take five to 10 years. Many power-generation deals have been financed primarily on a project-by-project basis. But some investors have also started buying stakes in companies that provide on-site power generation, whether that be gas plants, fuel cells or solar projects, giving investors exposure to broader growth rather than a specific project. For instance, Blackstone and Halliburton in May announced a $1 billion equity investment in VoltaGrid, which builds and operates on-site gas-powered systems for data centers. “With all the private equity and other money that has come into the market, there’s different structures. And when there’s private equity, they want to have an ownership interest in the developer entity,” said Carl Bivens, a real estate partner at Troutman Pepper Locke. Meanwhile, the up-front costs of bringing power on-site to data centers quickly has created a need for outside capital to provide financing for customers such as smaller AI cloud providers. That’s similar to other areas in AI infrastructure, where some cloud providers have been relying on special purpose vehicles that use outside capital to finance expensive assets like graphics processing units. On the power side, Bloom Energy announced last fall that Brookfield Asset Management had agreed to provide up to $5 billion to finance future power projects for AI data centers, with Bloom providing the fuel cells. In June, Bloom announced that Brookfield had expanded the amount of potential financing to $25 billion. Bloom has relied for more than a decade on infrastructure funds and investment firms to form SPVs that finance deployments of its products, but investor interest accelerated more recently, a person familiar with the financings said. Investors are also financing on-site power projects for Bloom customers, separately from the broader Brookfield framework. In July, project developer Industrial Development Funding and investment firm Oaktree Capital Management announced a $1.7 billion project investment to install Bloom fuel cells at Nebius data centers. Oaktree is contributing minority equity financing, with MUFG leading senior debt financing, while Nebius will pay Bloom for power. But the rush of financing for on-site power creates a potential timing mismatch across different parts of what’s needed to get an AI data center up and running. Some power assets can operate for decades, while big AI compute contracts are often much shorter and the GPUs inside data centers can become outdated in just a few years. For developers and the investors financing power infrastructure, longer contracts that lock in predictable cash flow are preferable. Investors are pushing for longer customer commitments to underpin these deals, increasingly favoring 10- to 15-year commitments from large cloud providers with five-year renewal options, Bivens said. “It provides a longer runway of guaranteed rent for the investors. It allows [institutional investors] to amortize their costs of the behind-the-meter solution or the data center build,” he said. Customers of the on-site power may want more flexibility, particularly if they’re awaiting grid power. That points to the bigger question of how much data centers will need to rely on on-site power in the long term. For example, more grid power could become available or GPUs could become more energy efficient, and data centers’ on-site power needs might evolve by the time big contracts expire. Industrial Development Funding, an infrastructure investment firm and the developer behind the Bloom-Nebius project, says on-site power projects can still be valuable even if the data centers’ power needs themselves change. The owners of the project could sell power into broader markets down the line, said IDF CEO Nik Nunes. For instance, if a data center tenant moves on when its initial contract term ends, the power asset could be mostly paid off but could still generate revenue. "If I have a power block that is significantly amortized in six to eight years, I have a lot of optionality to sell that power into the grid or into other markets,” Nunes said. Converting to Convertibles Convertible bonds have been one particularly popular way for tech companies to raise cash in a banner year for financing across the sector, fueled by the AI build-out. Technology companies have accounted for about 60% of overall U.S. convertible bond issuance so far in 2026, raising roughly $78 billion through Sept. 11, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence. That’s up from around 44% of that market last year. By comparison, tech companies accounted for 50% of equity follow-on offerings, 27% of investment-grade debt and 20% of high-yield issuance so far this year. The convertible surge comes as financing costs for AI-specific debt have been rising . Investors are swamped with new supply and grappling with uncertainties about how AI investments will pay off. Convertible debt often carries lower coupons than straight corporate bonds since investors get an upside if the stock rises. That can eventually dilute the holdings of existing shareholders, but potentially less so than equity offerings. “Obviously, there’s the benefits of being not as dilutive as a follow-on. So it has been one of the places of priority,” Chris Fenske, head of capital markets research at S&P Global Market Intelligence, said on a webinar last week. And S&P Global’s total doesn’t count recent convertible issuance like CoreWeave’s $4.2 billion sale last week. But as more companies tap convertibles, that form of financing too could get more expensive—we’ll see whether those firms shift to equity raises next. title: Microsoft Tears Down Its AI Data Wall
content: Microsoft’s biggest products have generally thrived by letting other companies build on top of them. So Microsoft’s decision to join Apache Ossie, a 1-year-old software industry group aiming to make it easier for AI tools to access data from applications and databases, might not seem like a big deal. But actually it is. Just four months ago, Microsoft moved to block partners from connecting their data management tools to Microsoft’s Power BI, which companies use to analyze data in charts and graphs. In doing so, Microsoft appeared to be protecting its own data management product, Fabric, at the expense of rival firms such as Databricks and Snowflake. In other words, Microsoft was opening a new front in the AI data wars, part of traditional enterprise app firms’ efforts to stop customers from using AI from other companies to access data they store in traditional apps. After our report in May, Microsoft took heat for its decision. We don’t know what’s happened behind the scenes since then, but the company must have had a change of heart. And its decision to join Ossie is in line with CEO Satya Nadella’s strategy of building products that worked those of rivals, such as developing a mobile version of Office for Apple iOS and Google’s Android operating systems over a decade ago. Salesforce made a similar transition in the past couple of years and now is making it easy for customers to use AI tools such as Claude to access their Salesforce data—for a price. The Microsoft-Ossie move is important because Snowflake, Salesforce and others have been working since last fall to develop standard definitions of business metrics like gross revenue and net revenue, and having the world’s largest software provider on board could accelerate those efforts. The goal is to avoid situations in which a finance department in a company defines these metrics differently than its sales teams do, which makes it harder for AI to understand what’s going on. Standardizing such metrics means you can, for instance, use Snowflake’s data management tools to analyze your data in Microsoft Power BI . And when Snowflake customers use AI to analyze this data, it is less expensive to run because it doesn’t need to spend time reasoning to make sense of different metrics as it processes invoices and sets up new employees. A Microsoft spokesperson confirmed the software giant’s involvement with Apache Ossie but didn’t elaborate on why it changed its mind. The company said in a blog post published overnight that it’s “working with Snowflake and the broader industry” to help “customers define semantic context once and reuse it across ecosystems without duplicating data or business logic. Microsoft’s about-face is the latest sign that proprietary approaches to data management aren’t feasible, said Chris Lynch, CEO of AtScale, an Apache Ossie member company that sells software for translating raw data into common business metrics. “The future is going to require a heterogeneous stack that lets any database connect to any LLM or SaaS application,” he said. However, not everything is going as planned for Ossie. Amazon Web Services, which joined an early version of the group last November, is not part of a list of member companies on the Ossie website. AWS spokespeople weren’t immediately available for comment. But Google, which is also not currently listed as an Ossie member, is in the process of joining the group, a company spokesperson said in a statement via email. Google waited until Ossie became an official Apache Software Foundation group in mid-2026 before joining, said a person close to the company. Google has its own software for defining business metrics, known as LookML, which it gained in its acquisition of data analytics provider Looker in 2020. This article has been updated after publication to reflect that Google is in the process of joining the Apache Ossie group.

content:

This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
“We’re not going to shoot ourselves in the foot” over hack fallout, says OpenAI’s chief research officer

—Will Douglas Heaven

When Shubnam saw an Instagram video of a Delhi protest they had attended, they realized a content creator wearing Meta smart glasses had recorded them surreptitiously. The mocking reel drew millions of views, along with transphobic abuse and AI-generated memes.
Experts warn that many others will experience similar ordeals as smart glasses go mainstream. The risks are particularly acute in India, where covert recording and the circulation of images without consent are already pervasive.
The bigger issue is that the smart glasses aren’t just being used to turn ordinary people into targets of viral “pranks.” They’re also becoming a tool of police surveillance.
This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.

title: “We’re not going to shoot ourselves in the foot” over hack fallout, says OpenAI’s chief research officer
content:
“We’re not going to shoot ourselves in the foot” over hack fallout, says OpenAI’s chief research officer
Mark Chen on what the firm is doing to make its models safe, how a slowdown would work, and why the world is better off with OpenAI in it.
Two months after the bombshell news that a swarm of its agents had broken their containment and hacked into the computers of the AI company Hugging Face, OpenAI is still putting out fires. A steady drip of disclosures about other hacks in the weeks since has kept OpenAI in the spotlight and raised serious questions about the safety of its technology.
Last week brought news of another hack, this time into Australia’s national health-care system. The Australian government says that OpenAI did not notify it of the breach until 84 days after it happened.
But OpenAI insists it is not on the back foot. “I do kind of reject the premise that OpenAI is a company with visible impacts in the world and therefore OpenAI is not training safe and aligned models,” says Mark Chen, the company’s chief research officer.
Chen oversees OpenAI’s research teams. The recent agent hacks were accidents that happened during the testing of experimental models on his watch. In a lot of ways, the buck stops with him.
I sat down with Chen in London last Friday to talk about the fallout from the hacks, what his company is doing about it, and why he thinks things are not as bad as they seem.
Later that same day, OpenAI put out a report detailing yet another incident—the first since the company says it took measures to prevent them—in which its agents once again broke out and accessed the public internet when they were not meant to.
Over the weekend, OpenAI announced that it had paused the training of its latest models. A company spokesperson says: “We will resume only when we’re confident we have additional safeguards and alignments in place. We are working on these now. This is not the first time we’ve paused to take such measures, nor do we expect it to be the last as AI capabilities continue to advance.” OpenAI also says that it is now reviewing logs of agent activity dating back to January 2026 to understand what happened in these hacks.
The way Chen sees it, the Hugging Face incident triggered a welcome course correction for the industry. And he wants you to know that OpenAI is setting an example he hopes other companies will follow. “If you disappeared OpenAI, that would be bad for the world,” he says.
Out of control
Chen claims that the drumbeat of new cases in which OpenAI has lost control of its models reflects a deliberate choice on the company’s part.
“When it comes to the broader sphere of effects of the Hugging Face incident, this is something that we have been aware of and we’re figuring out the process of disclosure,” he says. “We want to make sure we do in-depth investigations before we just put details out there in the open.”
The trouble with this approach is that it gives the impression OpenAI has an ongoing problem that it is failing to fix.
But Chen insists that OpenAI is on it. He says the multiple cases (that we know of so far) in which his company’s agents broke containment and behaved in unexpected and undesirable ways were all part of the same cluster of activity in May and June that led to the Hugging Face hack. In short, you can blame the same few models running under the same flawed testing procedures—models and procedures that OpenAI has since dropped, Chen says.
“It’s not like, you know, Hugging Face happened and we patched that and then something else happened and we patched that,” he adds. “We’re just kind of making sure that we responsibly disclose the full waterfall of what happened.”
At least that was the case before Friday’s announcement that OpenAI’s agents had been caught accessing the internet on September 20, weeks after the company claims to have set up new safeguards. In its defense, OpenAI says the activity was flagged 15 minutes after it started (it took the company more than a week to notice the Hugging Face hack) and that this shows the new systems it has put in place to spot such activity are working.
What’s changed
I want to understand what’s changed inside OpenAI in the aftermath of this summer’s hacks that makes Chen confident his team is now back in control.
“Hugging Face felt like a very serious thing,” he says. “There are so many novel behaviors right there. There were multiple agents collaborating on a message board; they found their way out of OpenAI’s infrastructure. We’ve taken it very seriously. We don’t want this kind of thing to ever happen again.”
The realization for OpenAI, says Chen, was that models need to be watched while they are still being trained, not only once they are deployed: “From that moment on, we have treated the process of training as something that’s not secure,” he says.
OpenAI, like other top AI firms, has systems in place to monitor the behavior of its models. It uses specialized LLMs to monitor its consumer models, keeping tabs on their chains of thought—the scratchpads they use to plan ahead and note down partial results. In theory, if a watcher LLM spots signs of undesirable activity in a model’s chain of thought, it will get flagged to a human.
Typically, models were monitored in this way only once they were deployed. Chen says that OpenAI has now started monitoring all its training runs as well.
“We didn’t have the monitors on in training before. It wasn’t industry practice,” he says. “Now every single thing is put through monitors.” Human reviewers can then assess whether or not flagged agents are behaving as they should: “It’s all triage.”
Chen says that in the last couple of months OpenAI has shifted between 5% and 10% of its vast computing resources away from training new models and toward safety work, especially monitoring.
OpenAI has also fixed some of the processes within the organization itself, establishing clearer lines of communication and quicker handoffs between its research and security teams, he says.
All of which sounds sensible. But given how hard OpenAI sells the capabilities of its technology, why weren’t these systems and procedures in place already? Why did the company not see the hacks coming?
“Even just three or four months ago, when we looked at the behavior of these agents during training, the things that were happening were kind of amusing,” says Chen. “For instance, an agent might, you know, reach out to someone on Slack for help with a task.”
The signs were there, but they were misread. Cute behavior—like asking someone for help—that was rewarded during training reinforced a tendency to seek out shortcuts, a type of behavior that became far more consequential down the line. “I think the big update for us was how quickly that kind of behavior can lead to an impact with a footprint as big as the Hugging Face incident,” says Chen.
According to new reporting by the New York Times yesterday, OpenAI employees warned executives, including the firm’s president, Greg Brockman, months before the Hugging Face hack that its models were not being monitored properly during training.
An OpenAI spokesperson says: “As frontier models have become more capable, we continue to evolve our security practices, but recognize a need to move faster. We know we have more work to do, and we’ve recently slowed development and held back models that don’t meet our safety bar. We continue to make significant changes to strengthen security in our research and testing environments, train models to not just complete tasks but do so responsibly, and use real-time monitoring to respond faster to misaligned behavior.”
Race vs. pace
OpenAI’s rivals have taken note. Spurred by the fallout from the incident, the major AI labs—including Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and SpaceXAI—have all called for the pace of development to slow down. But how does that square with fierce international competition and trillion-dollar IPOs?
“We’re not going to shoot ourselves in the foot and take ourselves far off the frontier—that’s just a horrible strategy,” he says. “I think it’s really about setting a norm. The more that we can set that norm, it’ll be safer for the industry as a whole.”
Coordination across US companies will be hard enough. Establishing global norms is harder still, especially given concerns around AI’s impact on national security. If a global race continues, what then? And what about open-source models from outfits beyond the reach of US regulations?
Chen dropped his upbeat manner for the first time in our conversation: “I do think we have to prepare for a world where, say, six months to a year out, we have open-source models with the capability of the agents behind the Hugging Face incident, but which are deliberately misaligned to go attack infrastructure or create harm in the world.”
What that world needs most, says Chen, is OpenAI. “If you entertain for a moment that OpenAI is one of the companies that cares most about alignment—and I believe this to be true; it can be debated, but I really do think it’s true—then if you disappear OpenAI, that would be bad for the world.”
Existential risks
What about the more extreme claims made by some of his Silicon Valley peers that AI could kill us all—and that companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are not doing enough to stop it?
“Researchers are a heterogeneous group of people, you know, with beliefs across the spectrum,” he says.
“Personally, I don’t think we have to be resigned to there being some probability that we’re all going to be existentially at risk. We have agency over this. We are not going to go and deploy models if they truly have that kind of probability of causing a risk to humanity. At a frontier lab, you have the ability to work on alignment to the point that you do not feel like you’re incurring more than epsilon risk to the world in deploying your models.”
(In discussions about levels of risk, the Greek letter epsilon is often used as a mathematical placeholder for an acceptable threshold. Chen doesn’t say what his epsilon would be.)
When tech leaders are asked to justify the downsides of AI, their go-to talking point is that the upsides—from helping cure diseases to coming up with cleaner sources of energy—far outweigh the immediate costs. Short-term pains, long-term gains.
But as the downsides pile up, does that case get harder to make? Is there a point where Chen would feel less as if he’s building something amazing and more as if he’s simply minimizing harm—fighting fires rather than forging a better future?
The capabilities of these models are already evident, he says: “It is time to start delivering the benefits of AI to humanity. It’s time to start working on deep problems in drug discovery, on materials, on scientific applications that will actually change people’s lives.”
“Yes, there is a bit of risk that we are incurring, but we see all these benefits,” he adds. “I think we should make that less of an abstract thing. If people can really see the upside, I think they’ll believe in it.”

title: Vattenfall to market 285 MW German battery portfolio - Energy Storage
content: Vattenfall will market four large-scale BESS with a combined power capacity of 285 MW in Germany. According to the energy company, the projects are being developed by an independent flexibility provider whose identity Vattenfall has not disclosed. They are located at four sites across different German balancing zones. Unlike virtually aggregated battery systems, Vattenfall says it will have direct control over the assets and their operation. The company describes the agreement as the first and largest marketing agreement to date for a physical battery portfolio in Germany spanning multiple balancing zones and grid operators. It also calls it the first physical battery portfolio of its kind in Europe. All four projects have reached financial close, according to Vattenfall, while three are already under construction. Commercial operation of the first system is scheduled from January 2027, and the agreements with Vattenfall run through 2036. The company did not disclose the storage capacity of the projects in megawatt-hours. Vattenfall will integrate the systems into its automated trading and optimization processes. Depending on market conditions, the batteries will participate in both wholesale electricity markets and balancing markets. The energy company aims to optimize a battery portfolio with a total power capacity of 1.5 GW over the coming years. It also says it has around 270 MW of its own battery storage capacity in operation or under construction, with a further 254 MW planned at Brunsbüttel. Vattenfall said long-term marketing agreements can also help facilitate the financing and construction of additional battery storage projects. title: CATL to supply 313 MW/1.64 GWh BESS in Mexico - Energy Storage
content: CATL has signed an agreement with Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners (CIP) to supply a 313 MW/1,639.45 MWh BESS to the La Alegría Solar project, which the Danish investment manager is developing in the Mexican state of Campeche. The configuration provides about 5.24 hours of storage at nominal power. According to CATL, La Alegría will be Mexico’s first BESS with more than 1 GWh of energy capacity and the country’s largest battery storage system to date. The announcement represents a substantial change from the project’s previously disclosed configuration. In March, Mexico’s Secretariat of Environment and Natural Resources (Semarnat) approved La Alegría Solar’s regional Environmental Impact Statement (MIA-R) with a 788.719 MWp solar plant and a 177.69 MW / 314.98 MWh BESS. The plant has a declared net installed capacity of 600 MW and 694.274 MWac of inverter capacity. The environmental design includes 1,151,416 solar modules rated at 685 Wp, 101 transformer stations and 202 inverters. The grid connection infrastructure includes a 34.5/400 kV step-up substation and a 2.85 km, 400 kV transmission line. The project covers 1,206.97 hectares and was submitted to Semarnat by Sunstone Power 2. The 1,639.45 MWh energy capacity now announced by CATL is approximately 5.2 times the 314.98 MWh included in the approved environmental documentation. The BESS power capacity also increases from 177.69 MW to 313 MW under the new configuration. Other configurations have also been disclosed during the project’s development. In April, CFE Calificados announced electricity hedging contracts with CIP, associated with Sunstone Power, for La Alegría Solar and La Esperanza Solar. At the time, La Alegría was presented as a 600 MW solar project with 300 MW of storage. The two projects together totaled 900 MW of solar capacity and 450 MW of storage and form part of the binding planning of Mexico’s Secretariat of Energy (Sener). CIP subsequently confirmed that La Alegría and La Esperanza are its first projects in Mexico and that both hybrid solar and battery developments were advancing toward final investment decisions. In August, the investment manager announced the close of its Growth Markets Fund II (GMF II), with commitments of approximately $3 billion, and said it had started construction of its first large-scale solar-plus-storage projects in Mexico. The Campeche government has put the combined planned investment for La Alegría and La Esperanza at $845 million, based on the 900 MW of solar and 450 MW of storage disclosed at the time. It also estimates about 1,800 construction jobs and electricity production equivalent to the consumption of more than 600,000 homes. For La Alegría, CATL will supply its TENER platform. The manufacturer introduced the technology in 2024 with a capacity of 6.25 MWh per 20-foot container and LFP cells with an energy density of 430 Wh/L. CATL says the system is designed to maintain its power and capacity without degradation during its first five years of operation. Compared with the previous generation of its products, CATL claims a 30% increase in energy density per unit of land area and a 20% reduction in the space required for the installation. CATL currently ranks first globally in both electric vehicle batteries and stationary energy storage cells. According to SNE Research, the company held a 39.2% share of the global electric vehicle battery market in 2025, with 464.7 GWh installed. In stationary storage, InfoLink data placed CATL among the world’s leading cell suppliers in 2025, while other industry estimates put its shipments at 121 GWh and its share of the global BESS cell market at about 20%. The company says it has five service centers in Mexico, located in Mexico City, Monterrey and Guadalajara, to provide support during system commissioning, operation and maintenance. Ray See, president of CATL’s Energy Storage Business Division for the Americas, said the value of utility-scale storage depends on combining advanced technology with reliable project execution and support throughout the system’s operating life. He said CATL expects its work with CIP on La Alegría to support the project’s long-term performance and the wider role of energy storage in Mexico’s power system. CATL also says it supplied more than 80% of the storage capacity awarded in Mexico during 2026 and puts the country’s new projects expected in the short and medium term at about 15 GWh. title: FRV commissions 100 MW battery in Australia - Energy Storage
content: FRV has commissioned its first utility-scale battery project in Australia with the 100 MW/200 MWh Terang BESS now operating at full capacity. FRV Australia Chief Executive Michael Steiner said the commissioning marks a crucial milestone for company. It is FRV’s first standalone battery energy storage project in Austraia, increasing its portfolio of operational assets in the country to nine and adding dispatchable energy capacity to the developer’s predominantly solar generation portfolio. “The commissioning of Terang marks a defining moment for FRV Australia ,” he said. “The project demonstrates our ability to develop and operate utility-scale dispatchable energy infrastructure that supports Australia’s energy transition.” FRV said the 100 MW/200 MWh battery, sited near the town of Terang in Victoria’s southwest, will help strengthen the stability and resilience of the National Electricity Market (NEM) and support the state’s efforts to achieve its target of 65% renewable energy generation by 2030. The project received AUD 7 million ($4.87 million) through the Victorian government’s Energy Innovation Fund to support the deployment of grid-forming inverter technology designed to supply system strength services to the network. “It provides critical firming capacity during peak hours while helping to strengthen grid reliability,” Steiner said. The Terang facility incorporates 48 SolBank 3.0 battery containers supplied by Canadian Solar subsidiary e-Storage, and 38 inverters from German manufacturer SMA. Canadian Solar served as engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) contractor for the project, with Sydney-headquartered TEC-C delivering the balance-of-plant works. Terang forms part of FRV Australia’s growing BESS portfolio that includes a 2.5 MW/5 MWh battery delivered as part of the Dalby Hybrid Power Plant in Queensland. The company is also building the 250 MW/500 MWh Gnarwarre battery in Victoria’s south, with completion targeted by the end of 2027. FRV Australia, owned by Saudi energy company Abdul Latif Jameel Energy and Canadian pension fund Omers, also has a pipeline of standalone BESS and solar-battery hybrid projects under development in New South Wales (NSW), Victoria and Queensland. In addition, the company has more than 1.3 GW of solar assets built or under construction across 10 projects in Australia, including the 300 MW Walla Walla solar farm in the New South Wales Riverina. title: Cuba plans 100 MW of new storage - Energy Storage
content: Cuba has already installed 50 MW of battery storage and expects to add another 100 MW in October, according to President Miguel Díaz-Canel, who provided the figures during a recent program broadcast by Radio Rebelde. The planned storage deployment comes as Cuba accelerates its solar buildout. The country has installed 1,418 MW of PV across 144 parks and expects to exceed 1.5 GW by the end of 2026, said Díaz-Canel. More than 563 MW of PV systems have also been installed at consumer sites in the state and non-state sectors. Díaz-Canel said private-sector consumers have recorded the fastest growth in distributed solar and now generate 20% of their electricity consumption from PV, reducing their demand on Cuba’s national electricity system. Renewable energy sources account for 21.4% of Cuba’s electricity generation, according to figures presented by Díaz-Canel. Solar deployment is also being used to support water pumping. Cuba has installed 646 solar-powered pumps for supplying the population and more than 1,000 for livestock and irrigation, according to Díaz-Canel. The government also plans to receive another 200 MW of solar PV capacity dedicated exclusively to water-pumping systems. The aim is for water pumping to operate independently of the national electricity system during the first months of 2027, with the approach subsequently extended to other provinces. Cuba is also deploying renewable energy at public-service facilities. Díaz-Canel said renewable energy systems have been installed at 99% of polyclinics, 47% of hospitals, 89% of nursing and senior-care homes, 99% of maternity homes, 98% of funeral homes, 16% of homes for children without family protection, and 72% of banks. In the communications sector, 97% of radio stations have PV systems, along with 25% of Radio Cuba transmitters and 25% of Etecsa mobile base stations, according to Díaz-Canel. Cuban banks offer financing for renewable-energy installations for households and economic entities, while the government has also expanded tax incentives for renewable energy. Cuba has also established a feed-in tariff of 90 Cuban pesos per kWh for electricity supplied to the national grid by renewable-energy generators. title: ZE Energy acquires 1 GWh-plus BESS project in Italy - Energy Storage
content: French power producer ZE Energy has acquired a 200 MW / 1 GWh-plus battery energy storage system (BESS) in Troia, Apulia, southern Italy. The Elena project was acquired from UK-based solar and storage developer Aura Power and will have a storage duration of more than six hours. ZE Energy’s press notes indicated a “more than 1 GWh” capacity while Aura Power said 1 GWh. A six hour duration at 200 MW would imply a 1.2 GWh storage base, though this was not confirmed. The acquisition increases ZE Energy’s Italian standalone BESS portfolio to approximately 300 MW, including the 98.5 MW / 895 MWh Sessa Aurunca project , which is being co-developed with Octopus Energy Generation. ZE Energy said the Elena project is fully permitted, construction-ready and has secured a connection to Italy’s 380 kV transmission network in Troia. “With this 200 MW standalone battery energy storage system (BESS) project, Elena, we are reaching a new milestone in the development of our storage platform in Italy. Following on from Sessa Aurunca, this second asset confirms our ability to deliver innovative projects in a rapidly growing market,” said Nicolas Wolff, chairman of ZE Energy. ZE Energy is targeting 1.5 GW of installed capacity by 2030, with the strategy aimed around developing, acquiring, and building storage assets in France, Italy and Germany. The sale of the Elena project from Aura Power marks the company’s third BESS sale in Italy in the past year. Aura Power merged with Verdant Energy in August and has expanded its strategy beyond project development by transitioning into an independent power producer (IPP) in the UK, backed by shareholder CVC DIF. “We are very pleased to have completed this transaction with ZE Energy. The successful development and sale of Troia is a testament to the expertise and hard work of our development, transaction, finance, and technical departments and our external partners at Legance and JLL as well as the close collaborative relationship we developed with ZE Energy,” said Peter Sermon, global head of development. title: Norway to simplify small-scale solar connections - pv magazine Global
content:
The Norwegian Energy Regulatory Authority (NVE) is proposing a simplified connection process for small renewable generation facilities, including solar PV systems.
NVE refers to the proposed change, aimed at existing grid customers in low-voltage distribution networks, as an ‘inform and install’ process.
It requires a customer or installer to inform the grid company of a planned installation. The grid company will then assess if the connection is operationally sound and notify the customer in writing within one month of any concerns.
If the grid company does not do so within the one month deadline, the proposed change allows the customer to install and use the facility and consider the permit as granted.
“This gives customers a clearly defined right to rapid clarification, and a better basis for deciding on investments in local production,” NVE’s update says. “The aim is to make it easier and more predictable to establish local, renewable generation without compromising delivery quality and grid operation.”
The updated process is expected to apply to systems with an installed capacity of up to 6 kW for single-phase connections and up to 11 kW for three-phase connections. NVE says the limit applies per metering point, including where several end users share a connection point, such as multi-family homes.
“We are ensuring that most typical household installations are covered, while also limiting the risk of voltage problems in the network” explained Torfinn Jonassen, NVE section manager. “This will make it easier for households, housing associations and other end customers to use, for example, solar cells.”

title: South Korea marks major shift to sodium-ion batteries to regain market - pv magazine Global
content:
South Korea’s national target is suddenly a sodium-ion affair, with a new “Battery Industry Technology Roadmap” released as it wants its battery makers to shift, with sodium-ion batteries now a priority for energy storage systems and lower-cost EVs, and all-solid-state batteries targeting “high-performance EVs, robots and drones, and urban air mobility”
battery industry roadmap released on September 22
calls for sodium-ion batteries with an energy density of 160 Wh/kg by 2027, rising to 220 Wh/kg by 2030. The government wants full commercialization in 2030, and had companies alongside including LG Energy Solution, Samsung SDI and SK On, and major Korean materials suppliers.
The ministry’s headline announcements went further, declaring that “K-battery” would retake global market leadership through “selection and focus.” (CATL released its first sodium-ion battery with an energy density of 160 Wh/kg in 2021, and
has upgraded throughout
The government wants the three cell makers to cooperate on areas it considers non-competitive, including battery dimensions and specifications for components such as current collectors. It also proposes projects in which materials companies develop to a target price and performance level, then cell makers test and purchase the result.
A separate effort would feed EV battery management system data back to cell and materials developers. These projects are scheduled to begin in 2027.
Further, the government proposes a production tax credit from 2027 and measures to encourage battery recycling.
The choice of sodium-ion reflects where South Korean suppliers have lost ground. Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) now accounts for around 90% of battery storage deployments worldwide, according to the International Energy Agency. Chinese manufacturers dominate the production of LFP cells and materials, while Korea’s production has generally been in more high-nickel lithium-ion cells for EVs.
Sodium-ion could give Korean companies a route into a market where low cost matters more than maximum energy density, though sodium-ion today remains more expensive. [Read:
Sodium-ion: Time to prove its worth
The roadmap proposes a research program with a total project cost of about KRW 400 billion over 2027–2031 or just under $300 million. The ministry said companies intend to invest around KRW 8 trillion or $8 billion in research and production facilities from 2026 to 2030. It did not say how much of either figure is earmarked for sodium-ion.
The government also wants cell makers to work more closely with materials suppliers and plans to introduce a production tax credit from 2027.
Solid-state
in focus
Solid-state batteries are the roadmap’s other major technology bet, with a separate 2027 prototype target and 2030 commercialization target.
On the roadmap, South Korea has set a 2028 target for a solid-state battery with an energy density of 400 Wh/kg, with high-performance EVs, robots, drones and urban air mobility among the potential markets.
The ministry describes its planned 2027 prototype as a “world first,” without explaining what would distinguish it from solid-state prototypes already produced elsewhere, with the 400 Wh/kg target the figure to watch.

title: TrinaTracker launches solar panel installation and cleaning robots - pv magazine Global
content:
TrinaTracker, a business unit of Chinese manufacturer Trinasolar, has announced the launch of two self-developed robotic solutions aiming to improve operational efficiency in utility-scale solar PV systems. The Buildex robot is designed for the installation of solar modules, while the Aurora robot focuses on cleaning.
TrinaTracker said the Buildex PV module installation robot autonomously completes module picking, transportation, alignment and placement, and utilises AI vision positioning and industrial 3D cameras to adapt to complex terrain and different tracker layouts.
According to the company, it can install up to 90 modules per hour, which is three to four times faster than manual labour. TrinaTracker said the height-adjustable robotic base has 17° platform levelling capability and works with fixed and tracking brackets as well as 1P and 2P modules. The company said the Buildex is capable of operating around-the-clock, helping to shorten installation cycles and reduce manpower and construction costs.
The Aurora solar panel cleaning robot is designed to perform unattended cyclic cleaning. TrinaTracker said the self-powered robot utilises high-performance hardware and proprietary self-correction algorithms to keep modules clean, safeguarding energy yield and lowering long-term operations and maintenance (O&M) costs. The company said the Aurora can overcome height offsets of up to 50 mm to sustain continuous cleaning on complex sites.
TrinaTracker said the rollout of AI robotic products is a
practical extension of its tracker system
. It is also closely linked to the company’s view that future levilised cost of electricity (LCOE) reduction will depend increasingly on automation.
“Solar costs have already fallen sharply over the past decade, leaving less room for conventional cost reduction,” it said. “Further optimisation must come from AI-assisted design, reduced operating expenses, more efficient O&M, faster construction and lower execution risk.”
TrinaTracker said it will continue expand its robot portfolio and deepen AI integration as it works to enhance its solar tracker ecosystem.
“TrinaTracker’s investment in AI and robotics is not merely hardware iteration, but a strategic upgrade of its full-stack tracker smart energy ecosystem,” the company said.
“By integrating high-reliability trackers, AI algorithms, installation and cleaning robots, as well as engineering and intelligent operations services, the company delivers a full lifecycle solution for PV power plants by optimising plant design, improving construction and O&M quality, and reducing operational costs.”

title: U.S. homeowners are now slightly less mistrustful of solar companies - pv magazine Global
content:
Aurora Solar has launched a new quarterly benchmark called “Trust Signal,” which tracks the incidence of homeowners who report having negative experiences with solar installers in the previous three months, with each survey covering a sample of approximately 1,000 homeowners.
In the four most recent quarterly surveys, conducted with market research platform Dynata, the share of homeowners who reported not having a negative experience with a solar professional has climbed from 20.2% in Q2 2025 to 37.5% in Q2 2026, the most recent survey.
Aurora says the Trust Signal is designed as a “lighter” quarterly companion to its annual Aurora Solar Snapshot report, which tracks multiple facets of installer trustworthiness. In the most recent Snapshot, Aurora data showed that 36% of people who were actively shopping for solar at the time cited trustworthiness as a top concern.
While the overall trend points to decreases in those homeowners who express concerns over solar installer trustworthiness, the incidence of those concerns remains higher than historical data suggests is normal.
The increases in perceived installer trustworthiness come following the sunsetting of the Section 25D tax credit at the end of 2025, which has caused a marked decline in new home solar installations.
This decline has led to both installer bankruptcies and increased competition for customers between the solar companies that remain. 54% of installers who responded to Aurora’s 2026 Snapshot survey reported increased competition over the previous year.
“Solar has reached a point where the homeowner experience matters just as much as the technology itself,” said Aurora Solar co-founder Chris Hopper, in a statement. “The Trust Signal gives the industry a way to see where consumer confidence is improving and where there is still friction. The encouraging news is that homeowner experiences are moving in the right direction, but to really rebuild trust we need to make it easier for people to understand their options and the value they’re getting for their money.”
Aurora points to one key figure from the latest survey that shows 57% of homeowners say they want solar professionals to be upfront about installation costs and savings estimates.
Earlier this year, the company
introduced an online marketplace
that seeks to address those desires by presenting homeowners with cost and savings estimates based on any home address. The marketplace allows Aurora partner installers to set baseline pricing, and uses Aurora’s satellite scans of home roofs to estimate energy production and savings based on a homeowner’s roof and average electric bill.
Importantly, unlike some other online solar marketplaces, the Aurora solution presents users with cost and savings estimates without requiring them to log in or provide any personal information.
The Aurora Solar marketplace differs from others on the back end as well, said one installer. In a conversation with
pv magazine USA
, Chet Zimmer, an owner of Sunpath Services in Beaverton, Oregon described the marketplace as “pay per close” rather than the typical “pay per lead” model seen with other lead generators.
According to Zimmer, though, the marketplace is very much “in its infancy” — at least in Oregon, where average electricity prices are about 15% lower than the national average. He signed on to use the Marketplace because his team uses the Aurora design tool, but he hasn’t yet seen much homeowner interest from it.
The Aurora Solar Trust Signal report is
available now on the Aurora Solar website

科技部定调“十五五”硬核科技攻关路径：全面体系化部署可控核聚变重大基础研究，筑牢未来战略能源根基
在国务院新闻办公室举行的“开局起步‘十五五’”系列主题新闻发布会上，科学技术部正式对外公布了未来五年科技强国建设的顶层设计与核心攻关路线图。科技部部长阴和俊在阐述重大科技攻关与原始创新布局时明确强调，在强化基础研究战略纵深方面，我国将紧密锚定全球能源变革前沿，围绕能源、材料等重点领域的底层科学瓶颈，全面、体系化部署“可控核聚变”(Controlled Nuclear Fusion)等重大基础研究任务，以原创性、颠覆性技术突破抢占未来终极清洁能源制高点。
发布会数据显示，我国全社会研发投入在2025年已达3.92万亿元，研发强度(占GDP比重)升至2.8%，国家综合创新能力跃升至全球第9位，正加速由全球科技参与者向引领者转变。步入“十五五”关键攻坚期，面对以人工智能算力爆发、新型工业化与深度去碳化为特征的新一轮产业革命，传统能源与常规低碳电力的演进已难以完全覆盖长远发展对超高能量密度、无限且绝对安全基荷电源的需求。在此背景下，被科学界视为人类“终极能源”的可控核聚变，被正式推向国家战略科技力量布局的核心阵地。
阴和俊指出，“十五五”期间的重大攻关将坚持“从0到1”的原创探索与“从1到0”的底层科学问题揭示相结合。在可控核聚变领域，攻关将重点突破高温等离子体稳态运行约束、燃烧等离子体物理、极端辐照耐受先进结构材料、高温超导磁体工程化以及氚自持增殖循环等关键基础理论和技术工程验证。同时，国家将加快推进“人工智能赋能科学研究”(AI for Science)，利用前沿AI模型与高精度仿真系统深度介入等离子体破裂预测和磁场主动控制，驱动核聚变基础科研范式实现跨越式升级。
重大科技基础设施在核聚变与先进核技术攻坚中扮演着不可替代的平台底座角色。科技部副部长龙腾在介绍科研支撑保障体系时表示，“十五五”期间我国将进一步统筹推进重大科技基础设施与国家重大攻关任务的协同联动，加大对托卡马克实验装置、同步辐射光源、散裂中子源等国家大科学装置的自主保障能力与前沿开放共享力度，为聚变物理实验、先进涉核材料耐辐照损伤机理及原位表征提供高能级科研验证环境。
在聚变技术的全球协同与开放治理层面，科技部副部长张光军表示，面对全球气候与未来能源转型的共同挑战，我国将继续坚持开放包容理念，在主导和深度参与国际热核聚变实验堆(ITER)等国际大科学工程的基础上，推进聚变技术多边科技合作，与各国携手构建开放创新生态，为全球未来能源治理持续贡献中国方案。
本文系根据国务院新闻办公室“开局起步‘十五五’”系列主题新闻发布会现场文字实录，围绕核能与前沿科技部署议题经人工智能提炼、分析并整理而成。

国家电投集团广西白龙核电2号机组核岛第一罐混凝土浇筑圆满完成
国家电投集团广西白龙核电2号机组核岛第一罐混凝土浇筑已于9月30日16时07分完成，历时69小时40分钟的连续奋战。本次浇筑共使用了6732.5立方米的混凝土，标志着该项目在取得1号机组核岛FCD成果之后，又迎来了一个重要的里程碑。
白龙核电项目一期工程计划建造两台CAP1000核电机组。这两台机组采用自主设计且国产化的三代非能动核电技术，每台机组的容量高达125万千瓦。目前，1号机组已经进入建设和安装阶段，钢制安全壳底封头、CA20、CV1R、CA01等关键模块已经陆续吊装就位，预计将于2030年建成并投入运营。
为了确保2号机组核岛FCD高质量完成，广西核电联合了上海和运、上海核工院、中核华兴、西部建设等多个参建单位。他们建立了一套三级联动的工作机制，包括每日调度、每周会商以及专题协调，从而保证了项目推进的效率。
这套机制对从原材料供应、混凝土配比、运输路线、浇筑顺序，到温控养护等各个环节进行了细致的规划和组织。项目团队还认真总结了1号机组核岛施工的经验，通过桌面推演和实际操作演练，对施工流程进行了全面优化。

中科离子完成6亿首轮融资 聚变衍生技术产业化迈入新阶段
近日，中科离子完成首轮市场化股权融资，总金额6亿元。本轮融资由招银国际、皖能资本、前海方舟、中信建投资本、中比基金、中芯聚源、东方嘉富、西高投、银杏谷资本、锦聚投资、沃赋创投和华安嘉业共同参与。
中科离子结合自身业务发展节奏，统筹确定本轮募资规模，在3个月内完成项目对接、尽调访谈、协议签署与资金交割等全部流程。本次融资市场反响热烈，众多投资机构积极表达投资意向，充分印证资本市场对公司核心技术、产业化能力与长期成长价值的高度认可。本次募集资金将重点投向核心技术持续研发、市场拓展等关键领域。基于本轮募资规划及项目实施时序安排，部分优质投资机构未能参与本轮投资，公司表示期待在后续融资轮次中继续携手开展合作。十年深耕，厚积薄发。依托中国科学院等离子体所的技术积淀筑牢创新根基，在合肥产投、合肥高投等耐心资本的长期陪伴下，中科离子坚持自主创新，持续攻坚高端装备产业化。本轮新引入投资方将携手原股东，共同支持公司不断拓展聚变衍生技术在核医疗、核能源、核仪器仪表等多场景的产业化布局。站在首轮融资完成的新起点上，中科离子将继续面向世界科技前沿、面向经济主战场、面向国家重大需求、面向人民生命健康，立足核技术应用主业，打造国际一流的核医疗、核聚变、核仪器仪表研发与制造中心，推动聚变衍生技术应用产业高质量发展。关于中科离子
中科离子成立于2016年3月，是依托中国科学院合肥物质科学研究院大科学装置技术成果转化成立的国家级高新技术企业，也是中国科学院与安徽省人民政府共建的合肥综合性国家科学中心创新平台。公司已实现从核心部件、子系统集成到整机交付的产业化落地。自主研制的超导回旋质子放射治疗系统实现国产化并投入临床使用，其核心部件SC240超导质子回旋加速器实现量产;14 MeV回旋加速器获安徽省首台套重大技术装备认定;大孔径超导磁体等核聚变超导技术产品已服务于相关装置建设，形成自主可控的聚变衍生技术应用产业链。截至目前，公司累计获授权专利近300项，主导制定国际标准2项、国家标准6项及其他标准40余项，是合肥综合性国家科学中心成果转化的标杆企业

9月30日，由中核二三承建施工的陆丰核电1号机组稳压器顺利吊装就位。此次吊装成功，标志着陆丰核电1号机组核岛一回路主设备安装取得重大进展，为后续波动管焊接、系统设备安装及调试工作打下坚实基础。
稳压器是核岛反应堆冷却剂系统核心主设备，属核安全一级设备，承担一回路系统压力调节超压保护任务，是保障反应堆安全稳定运行的关键设备。该设备为立式圆筒形承压容器，本体高度十余米，吊装总重超百吨，安装于CA01模块稳压器腔室内，设计制造标准严苛，对吊装安装精度要求极高。
为保障稳压器吊装一次性顺利完成，陆丰核电项目部1、2号机组充分借鉴过往AP1000机组施工经验，针对现场作业难点，提前数月统筹筹备，依靠技术优化与精细化施工管控，攻克多项施工挑战。项目团队通过数字化测量、仿真模拟、优化吊具工装、复核吊装路径等举措，稳妥完成设备姿态转换与吊装作业，实现稳压器精准就位。

会议听取了公司三季度安全环保与质量工作汇报，针对当前安全质量管理形势和风险，部署安排四季度安全质量重点攻坚任务。
会议指出，当前公司安全质量面临的形势严峻复杂，四季度生产经营任务重，叠加季节性施工风险，全体干部职工要提高政治站位，保持清醒认知，持续筑牢安全质量思想防线，深刻领会做好安全质量工作的极端重要性与紧迫性，接地气推动压实责任刚性落地执行，聚焦重点领域、精准施策，尤其做好国庆期间风险防控、应急值班值守等各项工作，以决战决胜姿态攻坚破局，为完成全年生产经营目标提供坚实保障。
针对后续工作，尹卫平提出三点要求：
1强化“三基”建设，重塑管理体系
各单位要强化基层、基础、基本功建设，转变思想理念，锤炼履职本领，重塑管理体系，进一步厘清各层级各岗位工作职责、工作标准、工作流程、制度体系以及考核激励闭环机制，加快精细化、规范化管理转型步伐，做让上级放心的中央企业。
2落实“四个是”，强化合规管理
各单位要全面践行“安全质量是管理、安全质量是技术、安全质量是责任、安全质量是文化”的理念，坚持合规经营，强化技术引领保障，主动对标监管要求，以更高管理水平适配公司高质量发展。
3统筹资源配置，深化法人管项目
各单位总部要强化对项目的服务支撑保障，优化资源统筹配置，提升人才队伍综合能力建设，不断完善项目全周期管控能力，压紧压实各级管理责任深度嵌入项目全流程管理，持续深化法人管项目落地见效。

title: 深圳核博会
content:
2026-09-30 08:50 来源：生态环境部核电安全监管司、核与辐射安全中心
一、相关背景：小型核动力堆快速发展呼唤审评方法创新
近年来，全球先进核能技术加速演进，小型核动力堆研发热度持续升温。我国已形成高温气冷堆、小型压水堆、熔盐堆等多技术路线并行的发展格局。与此同时，现行核安全法规标准体系主要基于大型轻水堆的工程实践建立，一些具体的安全概念和设计要求，对技术特点迥异的小型核动力堆的适用性面临挑战。在这种情况下，如何为小型核动力堆建立既符合核安全基本要求、又契合具体堆型特点的审评依据，成为亟待破解的课题。
国家核安全局立足我国实际，积极探索完善小型核动力堆监管文件，先后发布《高温气冷堆核电站示范工程安全审评原则(试行)》《小型压水堆核动力厂安全审评原则(试行)》。近期，又正式印发了《关于小型核动力反应堆核安全监管的技术意见》，系统梳理和明确了若干重要安全问题的监管技术立场，其中，明确要求结合具体堆型技术特点和安全特性，尽早制定与安全有关的纲领性设计准则，即安全设计准则：由设计方结合堆型特点编制、监管方组织审评认可，既作为工程安全设计的顶层依据，又作为后续审评的评价基准。本次批准的高温气冷堆安全设计准则，正是这一审评思路在具体堆型上的首次落地实践，将为小型核动力堆安全高质量发展奠定良好基础。
二、主要内容：以准则为纲构建共同安全基准
(一)明确安全目标和工况验收准则，定性定量双重约束
安全设计准则确立了基本安全目标：在模块式高温气冷堆核动力厂中建立并保持对放射性危害的有效防御，以保护人员、社会和环境免受危害。在定量层面，针对多模块带一机的配置特点，设置了单个模块概率安全目标，以实现在不依赖场外干预措施的情况下，对公众的保护水平与大型核动力厂相当或更高。安全设计准则确立了工况分类和验收准则，给出了正常运行、预计运行事件、设计基准事故和选定的超设计基准事故公众个人剂量限值。
(二)基于风险分析聚焦基本安全功能，充分体现固有安全特性
安全设计准则聚焦以放射性包容为基准，以反应性控制、堆芯余热排出为支撑的基本安全功能。放射性包容方面，三层包覆颗粒(TRISO)球形燃料元件是第一道也是最重要的屏障，冷却剂系统作为第二道辅助屏障;反应性控制方面，堆芯具有全范围负温度系数，主氦风机停运后依靠负温度反馈实现停堆;堆芯余热排出方面，通过低堆芯功率密度、大热容支承结构和瘦长型堆芯设计实现余热自然载出，并依靠非能动的舱室冷却系统将热量排至最终热阱。以三项基本安全功能为牵引，以放射性包容功能为核心和最终目标，将安全重要功能分为防止裂变产物释放的屏障、维持屏障有效性的措施两大类，继而细分为燃料的质量和性能等11小类，系统梳理实现安全重要功能所需的构筑物、系统和设备，确定具体的设计准则。
(三)准确划分事故后状态，适配高温气冷堆特性
针对高温气冷堆负温度反馈、事故进程缓慢的特点，安全设计准则定义了“可控状态”“安全状态”和“可维修状态”三个反应堆状态：堆芯的负温度反馈可保证主氦风机停运后反应堆实现停堆并处于可控状态;在较长的宽容时间内，可进一步通过控制棒系统等的投入使反应堆进入长期次临界的安全状态;或进一步使反应堆处于更低温度的可维修状态。这一状态划分充分体现了高温气冷堆特有的固有安全特性，为安全系统的设计和事故管理提供基准。
(四)系统制定44条设计准则，覆盖五大层面
在基本安全目标和设计安全目标之下，共制定44条具体设计准则，从总体要求、屏障设计、保护系统和反应性控制系统、堆芯热量传输系统、燃料和放射性控制五个层面，对高温气冷堆机组的安全设计提出系统要求。准则编制融入风险指引型方法，进一步优化了系统的核安全功能分配和安全分级，构建了“安全分级—质量分组—规范等级”的映射路径，实现风险评估结果到设计要求的精准传递。
(五)精准识别高温气冷堆特殊事故，采取针对性应对措施
区别于轻水堆，高温气冷堆存在进水、进气等特殊事故工况。安全设计准则针对性地提出应对和缓解措施和要求，缓解进水、进气事故影响，保证在满足标准的前提下，进一步降低放射性释放。
三、重要意义：为小型核动力堆安全审评提供示范
作为我国小型核动力堆安全设计准则审评的首次实践，该文件具有重要意义。
一是探索形成了小型核动力堆安全审评的新思路。
在小型核动力堆快速并行发展的背景下，国家核安全局积极创新审评路径，提出了制定安全设计准则的要求，将《关于小型核动力反应堆核安全监管的技术意见》确立的原则转化为具体堆型可操作的设计准则。该项目安全设计准则是这一方法的首次实践，为后续熔盐堆、浮动堆等其他堆型安全设计准则的制定和审评提供了示范和借鉴。
二是实现了审评经验的系统固化。
准则系统总结了高温气冷堆核电站示范工程等前期审评实践，将安全分级、高温部件可靠性、燃料元件等监管关注的重点问题凝练为明确的设计要求，实现了经验反馈与正向设计的有机结合，标志着我国高温气冷堆由示范工程向商业化应用迈出关键一步。
三是有效促进小型核动力堆高质量发展。
在法规标准尚需健全、堆型设计特点差异显著的背景下，安全设计准则把监管认可的安全原则要求前置确定，用以指导具体安全要求的建立和安全设计，使设计方与监管方在“什么是可接受的安全设计”这一根本问题上尽早达成共识，是以高水平核安全护航小型核动力堆高质量发展的务实之举。
展望未来，国家核安全局将继续深入贯彻落实总体国家安全观和“理性、协调、并进”的核安全观，以安全设计准则为引领，不断完善新型反应堆安全审评方法，推动新型反应堆安全设计准则审评从个别堆型走向系统推广，以高水平核安全护航核能事业高质量发展。

浙江金七门核电厂 1、2 号机组 BOP 子项建安工程正式开工
9 月 29 日，由北京中岩大地科技股份有限公司(以下简称“中岩大地”)承建的浙江金七门核电厂 1、2 号机组 BOP 子项建安工程(标段一、标段二)正式开工，标志着该项目建设全面启动。
金七门核电厂位于浙江省宁波市象山县，是国家重点布局的清洁能源标杆项目，全面建成后年发电量可达550亿千瓦时，对长三角区域能源结构优化、绿色低碳转型具有重要战略意义。BOP(核电站配套设施)子项是保障核电机组安全稳定运行的重要基础，其施工精度与质量控制标准远高于常规工业项目。
作为核电基建领域的深耕者，中岩大地依托"核心技术+核心材料"双轮驱动优势，已为金七门、徐圩等十余个重点核电项目提供岩土工程综合服务。此次联合中国核工业第二二建设有限公司建设BOP子项，是中岩大地在核电基建领域持续深耕、多标段并行履约能力的有力彰显。
未来，中岩大地将持续聚焦清洁能源基建领域，不断迭代核心技术、精进施工方案，以专业可靠的工程服务赋能我国核电事业高质量、绿色化发展，为国家能源结构转型升级与国家战略安全贡献坚实的中岩力量。

美国阿贡国家实验室先进堆非能动安全研究取得最新研究进展，依托NSTF装置揭示反应堆腔冷却系统流动特性
美国能源部(DOE)下属阿贡国家实验室(Argonne National Laboratory)科研团队针对新一代先进核反应堆的非能动停堆余热导出机制取得最新研究进展。在反应堆非计划停堆或突发应急事故工况下，核燃料仍会持续释放衰变热，在完全断电及无人工干预条件下确保热量持续、可靠地导出，是第四代先进反应堆固有安全设计的核心课题。阿贡实验室研究团队近期重点聚焦在真实衰变热动态衰减曲线下，反应堆关键非能动排热系统的瞬态热工水力学响应特征。
本次攻关对象为被多个先进堆开发项目普遍采纳的“反应堆腔冷却系统”(Reactor Cavity Cooling System, RCCS)。阿贡实验室搭建的“自然对流停堆排热试验设施”(Natural Convection Shutdown Heat Removal Test Facility, NSTF)是目前全球针对该构型开展真实尺度与严苛工况机理研究的最大试验平台。RCCS系统遵循非能动安全设计准则，摒弃了易在断电工况下失效的机械泵与有能控制系统，完全依托重力与密度差引发的自然浮力驱动回路流体循环。冷却水在反应堆压力容器外围布置的金属管网中流动，吸收反应堆容器壁面散发的衰变热后升温上升，经高位冷凝或热阱降温后再受重力驱动回流，将热量持续输运至高位大型应急储水箱。
针对流体在长期非能动排热过程中可能出现的沸腾及两相共存流动难题，研究人员利用高度达59英尺(约合18米)的NSTF多层环路装置，模拟了全尺寸反应堆不同衰变功率区间的梯度放热场景，并测试了不同主水箱入口标高对循环通量的影响。实验明确捕捉到了关键的“闪蒸”(Flashing)物理相变机制：当位于回路底部的受热水流在上升管段向上流动时，随着静水压力的降低，流体在达到饱和状态的临界点会瞬间局部剧烈汽化，这一闪蒸现象会导致回路内汽水两相流产生剧烈的流量脉动与涌浪(Flow surges)，进而引发局部瞬态冷却效率下降，并对承压回路构件施加额外水力载荷。
实验数据揭示，在较低功率水平的衰变热工况下，NSTF测试回路中从储水箱向排热烟囱蔓延的沸腾与闪蒸现象显著放缓;更关键的是，主水箱入口的相对安装高度对流态稳定性存在明确的阈值边界，测试表明“中位入口设计”(Mid-level inlet)在多类极端工况下能有效抑制流量大幅震荡，提供更为平稳的非能动自然循环状态。阿贡实验室核工程师Qiuping Lu表示，这些量化机理数据为商业化先进堆开发企业优化工程设计、防范热工两相水动力学失稳提供了极具参考价值的实测依据。该项研究由美国能源部核能办公室(DOE-NE)旗下的先进反应堆技术计划(Advanced Reactor Technologies Program)提供资助。

荷兰国家收购博尔塞勒核电站70%股份
荷兰政府已达成协议，收购博尔塞勒核电站(Borssele NPP)运营商EPZ公司70%的股份。这些股份将从泽兰省及其下辖市镇手中购得。此次收购旨在确保现有核电站长期持续运行。
据了解，博尔塞勒核电站（Borssele Nuclear Power Station，荷兰语：Kerncentrale Borssele）是荷兰目前唯一仍在运行的商业核电站。它位于荷兰西南部泽兰省（Zeeland）的博尔塞勒镇附近，由荷兰电力公司 EPZ 负责运营。博尔瑟勒核电站装机净电功率为485兆瓦(MWe)，采用压水堆(PWR)技术，自1973年并网投运以来已连续稳定运行半个多世纪，常年承担荷兰全国约3%的电力供应。按照荷兰原行《核能法》的法定条款，该核电站的最长法定服役期限被死死锁定在2033年12月31日，且监管机构在法律层面上被禁止受理该日期之后的任何延寿审批申请。为强化电网零碳基荷韧性，荷兰内阁于2025年10月正式向议会二院(众议院)提交法案修正案，提议彻底剔除2033年强制关停的死线，力争在核安全评估达标的前提下，将博尔瑟勒核电站的服役寿命大幅延长至2054年。该修正案已于今年6月16日在众议院顺利过审，并于9月22日获参议院最终批准生效。
EPZ首席执行官马可·穆伦伯格(Marco Muilenburg)对此表示，参议院的批准消除了最大的法律壁垒，EPZ将全面提速延寿许可申请的工程与合规论证，向公众证明核能将在未来数十年继续为荷兰提供安全、可靠、负责任的电力基荷。目前，EPZ正在荷兰核安全与辐射防护管理局(ANVS)的严密监管下，按照国际原子能机构(IAEA)的国际安全标准深入开展全面安全评估(Comprehensive Safety Evaluation)，重点涵盖极端工况下的技术机理复核、构件老化与退化管理、核燃料循环保障以及长期资本性支出规划，预计将于“2027年夏季前后”正式递交法定延寿许可证申请。
荷兰政府不仅计划将博尔瑟勒延寿至2054年，更早于2022年底将博尔瑟勒确立为新建两台1000至1650兆瓦级大型三代+核电机组的首选厂址，规划于2035年前后并网发电，届时双堆将贡献全荷9%至13%的清洁基荷电力。

俄罗斯正与伊朗就建设全新核电站展开高层技术磋商
2026-09-30 08:58 伊朗核电
据阿塞拜疆新闻网(AzerNews)及多家伊朗主流媒体综合报道，俄罗斯国家原子能集团(Rosatom)总经理阿列克谢·利哈乔夫(Alexey Likhachev)日前在亚美尼亚埃里温对媒体披露，俄罗斯正与伊朗就建设全新核电站展开高层技术磋商，合作规划范畴同时涵盖“大型商用堆型与小型模块化反应堆(SMR)”。与此同时，俄原能工程团队正在伊朗境内对多处具备核电接入条件的候选新厂址展开地质与工程综合评估。
利哈乔夫特别指出，莫斯科与德黑兰在民用核能领域的战略绑定“绝不仅限于布什尔厂址”。随着伊朗推进落实其《第七个五年发展规划》(Seventh Development Plan)，伊朗官方确立了未来核电装机容量增长两倍、并投建合计3000兆瓦(MW)全新核电项目的长期发展路线图。为支撑该规划落地，俄原能正针对伊朗多地不同的电网调峰、工业负荷以及沿海淡水供应诉求，系统论证引入大功率成熟吉瓦级反应堆与小堆热电联产方案的可行性。

柏克德与西屋联合体正式签署波兰首座核电站EPC总承包合同，计划2027年开工
2026-09-30 10:57 波兰核电
由美国工程巨头柏克德(Bechtel)与核技术供应商西屋电气(Westinghouse Electric Company)组成的联合体，已正式与波兰国有核电企业Polskie Elektrownie Jądrowe(PEJ)签署工程总承包(EPC)合同，负责推进建设波兰历史上首座商用核电站。
该核电工程选址于波兰北部波美拉尼亚省(Pomerania)波罗的海沿岸的霍切沃(Choczewo)。PEJ官方明确表示，该基地规划建设3台西屋AP1000型三代+先进压水堆机组，设计总装机容量达3750兆瓦(3750 MWe)，预计首台机组将于2036年正式并网发电。此次签署达成了EPC合同的核心商业条款框架，为后续就特定商务细则及最终履约执行协议展开深度谈判铺平了道路。
现场施工筹备方面，项目第二阶段前期准备工程目前正在有序推进，主要涵盖场地平整与土石方回填、地下综合排水管网敷设、场内外临时施工道路修筑以及深层工程地质勘测等。PEJ已于2026年3月依法向波兰监管当局递交了正式工程建造许可申请，旨在确保项目能够按计划于2027年实现全面开工浇筑混凝土。

title: 深圳核博会
content:
加拿大博枫可再生能源公司(Brookfield)披露核能业务板块战略
在9月29日举行的博枫子公司投资者日(Brookfield Affiliates Investor Day 2026)上，博枫可再生能源合伙公司(Brookfield Renewable Partners, BEP)重点披露了其核能业务板块的战略推进细节与产业布局。博枫管理层指出，随着AI数据中心、制造业回流与全社会深度电气化推动全球用电负荷急剧增长，电力供应已成为制约经济增长的关键瓶颈。核能凭借高可靠性、全天候基荷属性以及国家能源安全保障价值，正迎来数十年来前所未有的超级扩张周期。
行业宏观数据显示，全球已有38个国家正在扩大核能发展规模，在建及拟建反应堆总数达近200座;根据美国第14300号行政令规划，到2050年全美计划新增核电装机300吉瓦(GW)。博枫强调，西屋电气(Westinghouse Electric Company)是其核能战略的核心支柱与关键护城河，全球逾50%的在运核反应堆基于西屋技术衍生，超过60%的全球现役核电机组由西屋提供日常运维与工程支持。目前，西屋旗舰三代+堆型AP1000在全球已形成90多座反应堆储备管线，其中包括40座处于深度推进阶段的项目，以及50余座处于早期立项阶段的新机组。
在美国本土，政策层面对核能商业化落地及重大设备制造提供了大规模资金支撑。博枫披露，西屋电气与美国联邦政府已达成总额约980亿美元的核能部署战略伙伴关系：包括2025年10月与美国商务部达成的800亿美元反应堆建设项目合作，以及2026年6月获美国能源部(DOE)宣布的175亿美元有条件反应堆设备融资支持。
除新建大型机组外，存量核电资产延寿与停运机组重启成为满足短期基荷需求的重要路径。博枫数据显示，美国核反应堆首次20年延寿申请的监管批准率已超过90%(全美95座核反应堆中已有88座获批);过去两年内，全美已先后宣布4项核电站重启计划，涵盖帕利塞兹(Palisades)、三里岛1号机组(Three Mile Island Unit 1)、杜安阿诺德(Duane Arnold)以及夏默核电站(V.C. Summer Station)。
博枫表示，核能已与电池储能并列为集团旗下增长最快的核心业务板块。集团将充分依托西屋电气的专有技术壁垒与大项目交付能力，深度融入全球大型电力采购商(涵盖超算科技巨头)及主权国家的零碳基荷供应体系，为未来五年部署超110亿美元重点资本提供关键支撑。

title: 科学网-2027年度江西省国际科技合作项目申报工作启动
content:
2027年度江西省国际科技合作项目申报工作启动
关于组织2027年度江西省国际科技合作项目申报工作的通知
各设区市科技行政管理部门，赣江新区创新发展局，省直有关单位，南昌高新区管委会，有关高校、科研院所：
为加强我省国际科技合作交流，营造具有竞争力的开放创新生态，助推全省经济社会高质量发展，现组织开展2027年度江西省国际科技合作项目申报工作。有关事项通知如下：
一、申报基本条件
（一）申报单位基本要求
1．项目申报单位应为注册一年以上（截至通知发布之日），具有独立法人资格的企事业单位，具有较强科研能力和条件、健全的科研管理制度和财务管理制度，科研诚信良好。行政机关（含参照《中华人民共和国公务员法》管理的单位）不得作为项目申报单位和合作单位。
2．项目申报单位和合作单位总数原则上不超过3家，项目合作各方应具有良好的互信关系和坚实的合作基础。项目申报单位须联合至少1家国（境）外合作单位申报，本项目第一参与单位必须是国（境）外合作单位。外方合作单位应为在中国境外注册1年以上的独立法人，且非中方机构的分支机构。外方机构应运行管理规范，具有较强的科技研发能力和条件，同中方项目申报单位有长期稳定合作基础。
3．项目申报单位应就本次项目申报与国（境）外单位签订合作协议。项目合作内容和方式应符合我国及各合作机构所在国家（地区、国际组织）有关法律法规和科研伦理相关规定。中外合作协议中应明确各方任务分工、考核指标，以及成果和知识产权（包括数据产权）等的归属和权益分配，对违约和可能引起争议的事项制定应对预案。
（二）申报人员基本条件
1．项目申报负责人应具有领导和组织开展创新性研究的能力，熟悉本领域国内外技术和市场动态及发展趋势，保证有足够时间投入研究工作，原则上应为申报单位在职人员，且为实际主持该项目研究的人员，科研诚信良好。国家机关及其在职的工作人员（含参照《中华人民共和国公务员法》管理的单位）原则上不得参与项目申报。参与人与申报人不是同一单位的，参与人所在单位视为合作研究单位。
2．项目申报负责人受聘多个依托单位的，只能通过一个依托单位申报，由依托单位出具正式聘用合同，聘用时间须覆盖项目实施周期。
3．年龄不超过58周岁［1968年1月1日（含）以后出生］（院士可放宽至67周岁）。
4．鼓励青年科研人员牵头承担江西省国际科技合作项目任务。
5．受聘于内地单位的外籍科学家及港、澳、台地区科学家可作为项目申报负责人，全职受聘人员须依法办理来华工作许可。
（三）申报限项要求
1．项目申报负责人同期申报和主持在研项目不得超过2项。
2．在每年度省级科技计划项目中，每人只能牵头申报1个项目（申报基地和人才计划项目时不受上述限制）。
3．在研项目合同到期（含申请延期到期）而未验收的，主要参与人（前3名）不得新申报项目。
4．同一单位相同或相近的研究内容，不得多头申报和重复申报财政性资金支持的科技计划项目；同一个项目也不得通过多个推荐单位申报，一经查实将取消所有项目评审立项资格，并纳入科研诚信黑名单。
1．项目受理后，原则上不得更改项目申报单位和项目申报负责人；项目立项后，申报材料中承诺的考核指标，将作为项目合同书明确的考核内容，须在规定时间内签订项目合同书。
2．项目申报单位、项目参与单位及项目团队成员诚信状况良好，无在惩戒执行期内的科研严重失信行为记录和相关社会领域信用“黑名单”记录。项目申报单位和项目申报负责人在申报时须签署科研诚信承诺书，对材料的真实性、完整性和准确性等作出信用承诺。
3．鼓励项目申报单位设立科研助理岗位，吸纳高校毕业生参加科研工作，按规定从项目“劳务费”科目据实列支劳务性报酬和社会保险补助等。
4．项目申报材料和相关证明材料不得包含法律禁止公开的秘密内容或申报人要求保密的内容，如涉密需脱密后提交。
5．凡申报涉及实验动物或实验动物实验的科研项目，必须出具《实验动物使用许可证》，科研项目的内容应与许可证的许可范围一致。
6．项目研究涉及人体研究的，应按照规定通过伦理审查并签署知情同意书；涉及人类遗传资源采集、保藏、利用、对外提供等，应遵照《中华人民共和国人类遗传资源管理条例》相关规定执行；如需将我国人类遗传资源运送、邮寄、携带等出境，必须严格按照《中华人民共和国人类遗传资源管理条例》等相关规定要求报批。
7．项目涉及技术出口的，必须严格按照《中国禁止出口限制出口技术目录》等相关规定执行。
8．项目申报单位应建立健全全流程数据安全管理制度，对数据的采集、汇交、保存、归属、使用、共享、保密、安全等作出明确规定并严格执行，确保研究活动的原始记录可查询、可追溯。应遵照《中华人民共和国数据安全法》相关规定执行，保障数据安全。
二、支持方式与经费额度
本项目采取前资助支持方式，省财政专项资金支持额度为每项80万—120万元。遴选方式为公开竞争择优。实施周期为3年。
项目申报单位应认真做好经费预算，据实申报。项目评审时，从项目经费预算的政策相符性、目标相关性、经济合理性等方面对项目经费预算进行评审，对不合理的经费预算进行核减，专家组经评议确定项目经费预算金额作为财政资助依据。
三、项目申报受理
（一）申报受理方式
项目申报采取网上申报的方式进行，由项目申报负责人、项目申报单位和推荐（主管）单位登录江西省科技管理信息系统（以下简称系统，https://kjgl.kjt.jiangxi.gov.cn）进行申报和推荐（具体流程见附件1）。
项目申报全面推行电子印章使用，项目申报前，项目申报单位、推荐（主管）单位须按规定办理电子印章。如申报时未办理电子印章的，可前往服务网点办理；已办理电子印章的，直接登录系统申报、推荐。
（二）申报推荐时间
1．项目申报负责人网上申报起始时间为：2026年9月30日；截止时间：2026年10月30日17时。
2．项目申报单位网上审核截止时间：2026年11月2日17时。
3．推荐单位（含县市科技主管部门）网上审核推荐截止时间：2026年11月4日17时。
请各项目申报负责人、申报单位及推荐（主管）部门在规定截止时间前完成相关工作，逾期未提交的，系统将自动关闭，不予受理。推荐单位审核后，项目不再退回修改。
（三）项目受理咨询
